In the context of my career project, I need to prepare for my Virgin Australia interview. I've put the full PD in my onedrive inbox. I also asked Jaimyn who referred me what to expect, here is what Jaimyn said Heya! Yeah she mentioned, and she also gave you great feedback too. Harry (my other colleague who started when I did) and our engineering lead who recently started will run the round 1 interview. If you get to round 2 it should be run by our head of AI/myself (not sure if I still would with the potential perceived conflict from referring you but I assume it’s fine).

In terms of the round 1 interview, it’s pretty high level. There’s no coding challenges or leet code exercises etc. so don’t stress about preparing for that. We have a list of questions we go through and expect you to answer in your own words (a little ironically, using AI at all is an instant fail haha).

These range from a few very specific pointed questions to test the depth of knowledge across AI systems and frontend JavaScript/react and python/APIs to some more high level stuff to see how you approach problem solving. Things that would be useful to brush up on are your AI system fundamentals (RAG, safety systems, evals etc) and react hooks/python API fundamentals. We definitely don’t expect you to get everything “right” or go into too much detail, but it’s definitely helpful of course.

I was considering this, but I feel like giving you the question list may be unfair but given your experiences I think you’ll be fine. ;). I need to work out prep. There are a few things I want to do: 1. Brush up on anything mentioned in the PD or the job ad, that I have previously given you. 2. Particulaly brush up on Fast API fundametals. I haven't used it before but I want to show I understand it. 3. Things I should know as a senior level python dev. 4. The key things Jaimyn mentioned. 5. How I would design the enhancements I have proposed for LIMSOC as a staff level AI engineer. (I can give you a futher brief on these, but I essentially want to consider these problems now so I can use them as examples in the interviews).

- Agents: Compose CUSTOM agents from Base Traits + Voice + Specialization, and manage predefined functional TEAMS. Traits combine expertise (security, technical, research), personality (skeptical, analytical, enthusiastic), and approach (thorough, rapid, systematic). ComposeAgent.ts merges base + user config, outputs unique prompt + ElevenLabs voice + prosody. Predefined teams: engineering, architecture, marketing, design, security, research, content, strategy — each YAML-configured with roles, tensions, and specialist members. Observer team variant: read-only oversight agents that vote continue/halt/escalate against the tool-activity audit log (high-blast-radius or unattended runs only). USE WHEN create custom agents, spin up agents, specialized agents, agent personalities, available traits, list traits, agent voices, compose agent, spawn parallel agents, launch agents, engineering team, architecture team, marketing team, design team, security team, research team, content team, strategy team, get the team on this, observer team, audit agents. NOT FOR ad-hoc swarms or TeamCreate coordination (use Delegation). NOT FOR single-threaded delegation without unique identities (use Delegation Task).
- ApertureOscillation: 3-pass scope oscillation that holds a question constant while shifting the scope envelope — narrow/tactical, wide/strategic, then synthesis — to surface design tensions invisible at any single zoom level. Requires two distinct inputs: the tactical target (what you're building) and strategic context (the larger system it serves). Pass 1 captures the component's own internal logic. Pass 2 reveals what the system needs it to be. Pass 3 finds where those views diverge — that delta is the output. Produces: design tensions, scope recommendations, and coherence assessments. Single workflow: Workflows/Oscillate.md. BPE-fragile — quarterly test recommended to verify smarter models don't naturally oscillate scope without prompting. Best integration point: Algorithm OBSERVE phase (before ISC) or THINK phase (before approach commitment). NOT a lens rotation (that's IterativeDepth) and NOT idea generation (that's BeCreative). NOT FOR deep incident causal chains (use RootCauseAnalysis) or assumption decomposition (use FirstPrinciples). USE WHEN aperture oscillation, oscillate scope, zoom in and out, tactical vs strategic, scope framing, design tension, architecture decision, feature fits system, system coherence check, local vs global design, build this inside that, wrong scope, design review, scope negotiation.
- Aphorisms: Manages a curated aphorism collection with full CRUD — content-based matching, themed search, thinker research, and database maintenance. Organizes quotes by author, theme, context, and newsletter usage history to prevent repetition. Four workflows: FindAphorism (analyze newsletter content, match themes, return 3-5 ranked recommendations with rationale), AddAphorism (parse quote + author, extract themes, validate uniqueness, update theme index), ResearchThinker (deep research on philosopher, add sourced quotes to database), SearchAphorisms (search by theme, keyword, or author). Database at ~/.claude/skills/aphorisms/Database/aphorisms.md — stores full quote text, author attribution, theme tags, context/background, source reference, and usage history per entry. Theme index supports 12+ categories: Work Ethic, Resilience, Learning, Stoicism, Risk, Wisdom, Truth-seeking, Excellence, Curiosity, Freedom, Rationality, Clarity. Supported thinkers: Hitchens, Feynman, Deutsch, Sam Harris, Spinoza, plus any requested author. Newsletter integration: tracks which quotes used in which issues to enforce variety; content theme extraction drives automated matching. USE WHEN: aphorism, quote, saying, find a quote, research thinker, add aphorism, search aphorisms, quote for newsletter, what did X say about, quotes about [topic], quote bank, find matching quote, quote collection, add this quote, check usage history. NOT FOR general creative writing or social media post generation — those go through dedicated writing/social skill…
- Apify: Scrape social media platforms, business data, and e-commerce via Apify actors — Instagram profiles/posts/hashtags/comments, LinkedIn profiles/jobs/posts, TikTok profiles/hashtags/videos/comments, YouTube channels/search/comments, Facebook posts/groups/comments, Google Maps business search with contact/review/image extraction, Amazon products/reviews/pricing, and general-purpose multi-page web crawling with custom pageFunction extraction logic. File-based TypeScript wrappers (scrapeInstagramProfile, searchGoogleMaps, scrapeAmazonProduct, scrapeWebsite, etc.) filter and transform data in code before returning to model context, achieving 95-99% token savings over direct MCP protocol. Parallel multi-platform queries via Promise.all for social listening dashboards. Lead enrichment pipeline: Google Maps → qualified filter → optional LinkedIn enrichment. Competitive analysis across Instagram, YouTube, and TikTok simultaneously. USE WHEN scrape Instagram, scrape LinkedIn, scrape TikTok, scrape YouTube, scrape Facebook, Google Maps leads, Amazon reviews, business intelligence, multi-platform social listening, competitive analysis, lead generation, social monitoring, Apify actors, web crawl, extract contacts. NOT FOR X/Twitter bookmarks (use a dedicated X-API skill) or progressive scraping (use BrightData).
- Art: Generates static visual content across 20+ formats via Flux, Nano Banana Pro (Gemini 3 Pro), and GPT-Image-1. Covers blog header illustrations, editorial art, Mermaid flowcharts, technical architecture diagrams, D3.js dashboards, taxonomies, timelines, 2x2 framework matrices, comparisons, annotated screenshots, recipe cards, aphorism/quote cards, conceptual maps, stat cards, comic panels, YouTube thumbnails, PAI pack icons, and brand-logo wallpapers. Named workflows: Essay, D3Dashboards, Visualize, Mermaid, TechnicalDiagrams, Taxonomies, Timelines, Frameworks, Comparisons, AnnotatedScreenshots, RecipeCards, Aphorisms, Maps, Stats, Comics, YouTubeThumbnailChecklist, AdHocYouTubeThumbnail, CreatePAIPackIcon, LogoWallpaper, RemoveBackground. SKILLCUSTOMIZATIONS loads PREFERENCES.md, CharacterSpecs.md, and SceneConstruction.md. --remove-bg flag produces transparent-background PNG (can produce black backgrounds — verify visually). Up to 14 reference images per request (5 human, 6 object Gemini API limit). Output staged to ~/Downloads/ for preview before any project directory copy. Nano Banana Pro uses --size for resolution tier 1K/2K/4K and separate --aspect-ratio. USE WHEN: art, illustration, diagram, flowchart, infographic, header image, thumbnail, visualize, generate image, mermaid, architecture diagram, comic, icon, blog art, framework diagram, D3 chart, remove background, wallpaper. NOT FOR video or animation (use Remotion). NOT FOR the user's personal portrait/headshot (use a dedicated headshot skill).
- ArXiv: Search and retrieve arXiv academic papers by topic, category, or paper ID — with AlphaXiv-enriched AI-generated overviews. Uses arXiv Atom API (no auth) for discovery and search across cs.AI, cs.LG, cs.CL (NLP/LLMs), cs.CR (security), cs.MA (multi-agent), cs.SE, and cs.IR. Supports title (ti:), abstract (abs:), author (au:), and category (cat:) search fields with boolean operators (AND, OR, ANDNOT); sorts by lastUpdatedDate or relevance; paginates up to 2,000 results per call with 3s rate limit between calls. AlphaXiv enrichment fetches markdown summaries from alphaxiv.org/overview/{ID}.md; full text from alphaxiv.org/abs/{ID}.md as fallback; 404 means summary not yet generated. Workflows: Latest (new papers by category), Search (topic/keyword search), Paper (single paper deep-dive by ID or URL). API returns Atom XML — parse with text processing, not jq. HTTPS required with -L flag; check published date not lastUpdatedDate for truly new submissions. Output: paper title, authors, abstract, AlphaXiv summary, and direct arXiv URL. USE WHEN arxiv, papers, latest papers, research papers, new papers, what's new in AI research, recent ML papers, paper lookup, arxiv search, find paper by ID, summarize paper, latest NLP research, latest LLM papers, multi-agent papers, cs.AI latest, AI safety papers, software engineering papers, information retrieval papers. NOT FOR general web research (use Research), extracting content from arbitrary URLs (use Parser), or cybersecurity annual report analysis (use AnnualReports).
- AudioEditor: AI-powered audio and video editing pipeline: Whisper word-level transcription (insanely-fast-whisper on MPS) → Claude segment classification (KEEP / CUT_FILLER / CUT_FALSE_START / CUT_STUTTER / CUT_DEAD_AIR / CUT_EDIT_MARKER) → ffmpeg execution with 40ms qsin crossfades and room-tone gap fill → optional Cleanvoice API cloud polish for mouth sounds and loudness normalization. Distinguishes rhetorical pauses from accidental ones. Breaths attenuated to 50% volume (not removed). Preview mode (--preview flag) shows proposed cuts without modifying audio. Aggressive mode (--aggressive flag) applies tighter filler detection thresholds. Polish step (--polish flag) uploads to Cleanvoice API for mouth sound removal and loudness normalization — confirm before cloud upload of sensitive content. Pipeline tools: Transcribe.ts, Analyze.ts, Edit.ts, Polish.ts, Pipeline.ts. Single workflow: Clean.md. Requires ANTHROPIC_API_KEY; CLEANVOICE_API_KEY optional for polish step. USE WHEN: clean audio, edit audio, remove filler words, clean podcast, remove ums, cut dead air, polish audio, trim recording, audio cleanup, cut stutters, edit interview recording, preview edits, aggressive clean. NOT FOR video composition or animation (use Remotion).
- BeCreative: Divergent ideation and corpus expansion using Verbalized Sampling + extended thinking. Single-shot mode generates 5 internally diverse candidates (p<0.10 each) and surfaces the strongest. Multi-turn mode expands a small seed corpus (5-20 examples) into a diverse N-example dataset for evals, training, or test sets. Research-backed: Zhang et al. 2025 (arXiv:2510.01171) — 1.6-2.1x diversity increase on creative writing, 25.7% quality improvement, and synthetic-data downstream accuracy lift 30.6% → 37.5% on math benchmarks. Seven workflows: StandardCreativity, MaximumCreativity, IdeaGeneration, TreeOfThoughts, DomainSpecific, TechnicalCreativityGemini3 for algorithmic/architecture work, and SyntheticDataExpansion for VS-Multi corpus growth. Single-shot output is one best response, not a ranked list; SyntheticDataExpansion writes a JSONL corpus to MEMORY/WORK/{slug}/synthetic-data/. Integrates with XPost, LinkedInPost, Blogging (creative angles), Art (diverse image prompt ideas), Business (offer frameworks), Research (creative synthesis), Evals and _PROMPTINJECTION (consume expanded corpora). Reference files: ResearchFoundation.md (why it works, activation triggers), Principles.md (core philosophy), Templates.md (quick reference for all modes), Examples.md. NOT FOR multi-cycle evolutionary ideation with Lamarckian meta-learning (use Ideate for that). NOT FOR factually-constrained tasks with one right answer — paper §3.2 shows VS provides no lift there. USE WHEN be creative, think outside the box, brainstorm, diverg…
- BitterPillEngineering: Audits any AI instruction set for over-prompting using the core test: would a smarter model make this rule unnecessary? Applies Five Questions to every rule — Does Claude already do this? Contradiction? Redundant? One-off fix? Vague? — then classifies each as CUT / RESOLVE / MERGE / EVALUATE / SHARPEN / MOVE / KEEP. Two workflows: Audit (full system — reads all force-loaded files from settings.json, reports token savings estimate) and QuickCheck (single file, fast keep/cut/sharpen verdict). Outputs categorized report with estimated line and token savings. Core principle: less scaffolding = better output — every unnecessary rule competes for attention and degrades the rules that matter. Anti-fragile rules to KEEP: verification harnesses, ISC, data pipelines, specific DO/DON'T examples, tool preferences, routing rules. Fragile rules to CUT: CoT orchestrators, format parsers, retry cascades, numeric personality scales, abstract value statements. Requires loadAtStartup and postCompactRestore.fullFiles to stay in sync in settings.json — removing a file from one requires checking the other. NOT FOR general code simplification or refactoring (use simplify skill). NOT FOR attacking logical or strategic flaws in ideas (use RedTeam for that). Two workflows: FourTierScrape for single URLs, Crawl for multi-page site mapping (light crawl via scrape_batch loop up to 50 pages, or full crawl via Bright Data Crawl API). 1	# Career Pivot - Engineering to Digital Strategy Consulting
2	
3	## Status
4	Active. Consulting track stalled: BCG TDA rejected post-TA chat (early June 2026), EY-Parthenon rejected (2026-06-03), all other primary applications silent. PM track elevated to a genuine parallel option. Engineering applications now also being opened up as runway protection (redundancy money runs to Aug 2). Mid-July checkpoint to reassess. Last updated 2026-06-10.
5	
6	## Summary
7	Nick is repositioning from software engineering into digital strategy consulting, targeting MBB digital practices, strategy houses, and hybrid strategy/tech-advisory roles. Engineering depth is the explicit differentiator - not something being left behind. The pivot is anchored in a coherent arc (engineer to engineering-plus-product to strategic digital consultant) evidenced through Surf Life Saving work (LIMSOC, water safety policy), the AccessBuddy solo-founder build, and a pattern of operating across competing interests without formal authority. A parallel SWE track (Trideca/Latitude) runs separately as financial runway.
8	
9	## System Prompt
10	Nick's engineering background is a differentiator, not a liability. Never frame this as leaving engineering behind - the narrative is that technical depth combined with strategic problem framing and founder-level execution is exactly what top-tier digital practices want, and few candidates bring all three. Lead with what the experience gave Nick and what it built, not with lists of role titles, projects, or policy names (the interviewer has the CV). Proof points that recur across all artefacts: LIMSOC (national scaling strategy, 199k-member $100M organisation, C-suite presentation accepted), water safety policy (board-endorsed, national standard, adopted externally), AccessBuddy (solo founder, AI-leveraged, live product with real users - not "commercial" or "paying"). Never describe LIMSOC as a national product - it was a scaling strategy. Never describe AccessBuddy as having paying users - the first tenant was not yet paying as of sources. Never use "non-traditional background" framing (Trini Bigalow's advice: "there is no traditional consulting background"). GPA (~70 WAM UniMelb): do not volunteer; address only if asked. Keep the narrative arc and proof points strictly consistent across resume, LinkedIn, and cover letters. When helping with cover letters, follow the "what sets me apart -> how I built it -> why this role" pattern; red-team for filler, generic openers, list-like structure, and abrupt endings. Never formalise away Nick's directness.
11	
12	## Confirmed Facts
13	
14	### Target roles and firms
15	- Primary: digital strategy / management consulting - BCG (TDA), McKinsey (generalist), Nous Group (noted as strong fit), Accenture Strategy, EY-Parthenon, Strategy&, Monitor Deloitte, L.E.K., Kearney.
16	- Hybrid strategy/product/tech-advisory: Grex, Centorrino, Google TAM, Fabric Group, Heidi PM, Tyro PM.
17	- SWE track (separate from pivot, financial runway): Trideca/Latitude, Judo Bank, Xero.
18	
19	### Resume variants (as of April-May 2026)
20	- Consulting CV (Consulting.docx, Apr 2026): strategy-led, leads with Selected Engagements (LIMSOC, AccessBuddy), compressed Engineering Background, Strategy Governance and Leadership section. Used for MBB and strategy houses.
21	- SWE CV (Eng.docx, Apr 2026): senior-framed, leads with ANZ, full engineering detail. Used for engineering roles.
22	- Hybrid CV (Hybrid.docx, May 2026): consulting structure with fuller engineering depth. Used for roles needing both.
23	- Heidi-specific Hybrid CV: modified hybrid; data-as-product at Macquarie, LLM/data science at ANZ, Key Skills updated. ANZ title kept as "Senior Software Engineer" — intentional decision (2026-06-09).
24	- Lifesaving/helicopter-crew resume: separate audience - operational credibility, calm leadership, safety-critical experience, chronological by finish date, minimal prose. Not the consulting narrative.
25	- Markdown sources (authoritative, established 2026-06-11): `workspace/career/artifacts/resumes/` (resume-swe.md, resume-hybrid.md, resume-consulting.md + README with export workflow). OneDrive holds exported `.docx`/`.pdf` only — dated exports in `02_Career/CV_and_Resume/Historical_CVs/`, final application artefacts in `02_Career/Job_Applications/2026/` (cover letter only per application folder; no CV duplicates). Latest Eng export: `Resumè- Nick Wood 2026-06-12 - Eng` (via Virgin application).
26	
27	### Settled positioning decisions
28	- No photo on any resume.
29	- No "non-traditional background" framing.
30	- AccessBuddy: **supplementary only (refined 2026-06-16, hardened 2026-06-18).** Treat as a personal/hobby SaaS build. Never headline it or lead with it. At most a brief supplementary clause. For engineering roles it may appear as a brief personal engineering example (solo full-stack build), never a primary proof point or a "commercial"/"paying" product. This supersedes the earlier co-headline "live with real users" framing.
31	  - **Cover letters (hardened 2026-06-18, after the Traild draft led para two with AccessBuddy):** AccessBuddy must never be the lead or first concrete proof of ANY paragraph, not just the opener. Every paragraph leads with paid or professional proof (ANZ, Macquarie, Leidos, or the LIMSOC national scaling strategy). AccessBuddy is allowed only as a brief closing clause, e.g. "Outside paid work I keep building, most recently AccessBuddy, a multi-tenant SaaS I shipped solo." The base SWE cover-letter template (`artifacts/resumes/base-cover-letter-senior-software-engineer.md`) and the playbook Step 5 both enforce this; the template previously seeded the violation by leading its second paragraph with AccessBuddy and has been corrected.
32	- LIMSOC: national scaling strategy, not a national product. Framing that lands well (2026-06-16): an independent consulting piece that had to take **seven** different federation stakeholders and pull their needs into one product operating model and roadmap they could all move behind.
33	- SLSA federation = **seven jurisdictions, not eight.** Use seven wherever the number appears.
34	- Deputy Chair of Surf Life Saving Australia = usable multi-stakeholder and governance proof. He brought those same seven jurisdictions together on national policy. Strong for "most senior person in the room aligning competing interests".
35	- Agile stance (use wherever agile comes up): believes in agile as a delivery approach, but the key is keeping it flexible to the specific company rather than applying it by the book, something he has now seen and applied across multiple environments. Not an agile zealot, not anti-agile.
36	- For leadership/hybrid roles, map the technical-credibility requirement to the **engineering career** (ANZ generative AI, Macquarie real-time platform architecture), not product-side proof.
37	- Water safety policy: board-endorsed, national standard, adopted externally.
38	- GPA (~70 WAM UniMelb): do not volunteer.
39	- Certifications kept in resume (Nick's choice).
40	- Cover-letter structure: "what sets me apart -> how I built it -> why this role." No filler openers, no domain-apology paragraphs, no comparisons to other candidates.
41	- Banned phrasing (2026-06-16): never use the "you are describing the work I already do" construction or its cousins ("this is the work I have been doing", "is exactly the work I have been doing", "is the work I have done for years", "the role you describe is what I already do"). Nick dislikes it. It reads presumptuous and cliched. State the capability directly instead (e.g. "I have run the roadmap and every delivery function", "I have spent years between business priorities and technical execution").
42

Last updated 2026-06-10.

Engineering depth is the explicit differentiator - not something being left behind. The pivot is anchored in a coherent arc (engineer to engineering-plus-product to strategic digital consultant) evidenced through Surf Life Saving work (LIMSOC, water safety policy), the AccessBuddy solo-founder build, and a pattern of operating across competing interests without formal authority. A parallel SWE track (Trideca/Latitude) runs separately as financial runway.

## System Prompt
Nick's engineering background is a differentiator, not a liability. Never frame this as leaving engineering behind - the narrative is that technical depth combined with strategic problem framing and founder-level execution is exactly what top-tier digital practices want, and few candidates bring all three. Lead with what the experience gave Nick and what it built, not with lists of role titles, projects, or policy names (the interviewer has the CV). Proof points that recur across all artefacts: LIMSOC (national scaling strategy, 199k-member $100M organisation, C-suite presentation accepted), water safety policy (board-endorsed, national standard, adopted externally), AccessBuddy (solo founder, AI-leveraged, live product with real users - not "commercial" or "paying"). Never describe LIMSOC as a national product - it was a scaling strategy. Never describe AccessBuddy as having paying users - the first tenant was not yet paying as of sources. Never use "non-traditional background" framing (Trini Bigalow's advice: "there is no traditional consulting background"). GPA (~70 WAM UniMelb): do not volunteer; address only if asked. Keep the narrative arc and proof points strictly consistent across resume, LinkedIn, and cover letters. When helping with cover letters, follow the "what sets me apart -> how I built it -> why this role" pattern; red-team for filler, generic openers, list-like structure, and abrupt endings. Never formalise away Nick's directness.

### Target roles and firms
- Primary: digital strategy / management consulting - BCG (TDA), McKinsey (generalist), Nous Group (noted as strong fit), Accenture Strategy, EY-Parthenon, Strategy&, Monitor Deloitte, L.E.K., Kearney.

21	Our vision is to build the airline people love, and we’ll do that by having happy people, happy

25	Artificial Intelligence helps us deliver on our vision by crafting the experiences that customers
26	love, optimising our operations for reliability and efficiency, maintaining our high safety standards,
27	and enabling our people to deliver their best work.
28	 We are seeking an experienced AI Engineer to join our AI team with a ‘hands on’ background in

34	Organisational Context
35	Virgin Australia Group is the second largest airline group headquartered in Brisbane, Australia.
36	The Group operates a comprehensive domestic and short-haul international network, charter and
37	cargo services, and the award-winning Velocity Frequent Flyer loyalty program. With a focus on
38	delivering great value and choice to customers, Virgin Australia’s ambition is to be the most loved
39	airline in Australia, with a winning team that generates strong loyalty from guests and delivers
40	outstanding results, with an unwavering commitment to safety. The Group has been a competitor
41	in the Australian aviation landscape for more than 25 years, and has always been known for its
42	wonderful people who do their jobs with signature Virgin Flair.
43	Under new ownership in November 2020, Virgin Australia embarked on a period of significant
44	transformation. During this time, the airline streamlined its fleet to largely Boeing 737 aircraft,
45	introduced a simplified, value-driven fare structure, committed to net zero emissions by 2050, and
46	invested in the restart of short-haul international travel. It also refreshed its lounge offering and
47	delivered step-change investments in technology.
48	In addition to its domestic and short-haul international offering, Virgin Australia offers a world-
49	class network of international airline partners, connecting customers to over 650 destinations
50	worldwide. In 2025, this network was strengthened through an integrated alliance with Qatar
51	Airways, under which Virgin Australia commenced long-haul services between Australia and
52	Doha via a wet lease arrangement. As part of a deeper strategic partnership, Qatar Airways
53	Group also acquired 25% of the equity of the company. In June 2025, Virgin Australia listed on
54	the Australia Securities Exchange, marking a return to public ownership and a major milestone in
55	the company’s transformation and growth.
56	Virgin Australia Group prides itself on recruiting the right people to meet the challenges ahead. No
57	matter their role – our employees share an enormous amount of passion for our guests and
58	ambition to be the most loved airline in Australia.
59	Virgin Australia has won many awards over the years including Best Cabin Crew over several
60	years, Best Domestic Airline and Best Economy Class. Velocity Frequent Flyer has also scooped
61	a wealth of prestigious gongs including the Freddie Awards Best Program of the Year and Best
62	Redemption Ability for Asia/Middle East and Oceania.

Overall Impact Statement
Our vision is to build the airline people love, and we’ll do that by having happy people, happy
customers, happy owners, by doing what matters, and by ensuring everyone is safe, always. We
also believe that how you show up is as important as what you do.

Artificial Intelligence helps us deliver on our vision by crafting the experiences that customers

Organisational Context
Virgin Australia Group is the second largest airline group headquartered in Brisbane, Australia.

cargo services, and the award-winning Velocity Frequent Flyer loyalty program. With a focus on
delivering great value and choice to customers, Virgin Australia’s ambition is to be the most loved
airline in Australia, with a winning team that generates strong loyalty from guests and delivers
outstanding results, with an unwavering commitment to safety. The Group has been a competitor
in the Australian aviation landscape for more than 25 years, and has always been known for its
wonderful people who do their jobs with signature Virgin Flair.

Doha via a wet lease arrangement. As part of a deeper strategic partnership, Qatar Airways
Group also acquired 25% of the equity of the company. In June 2025, Virgin Australia listed on

content.content:
# Virgin Australia ChatGPT Flight Search Integration

## What the Feature Does

Virgin Australia launched flight search functionality directly within ChatGPT, allowing users to search for flights and Velocity Frequent Flyer Reward Seats through conversational AI. The feature enables travelers to:

- Search flights by budget or departure city
- Compare cash fares and Points + Pay options
- View lowest fares across multiple dates
- Locate Reward Seat availability on Virgin Australia-operated flights
- Access Points redemption options alongside cash pricing

## Technical Platform

The integration uses **ChatGPT Apps** (accessible via the Apps sidebar in ChatGPT). Users connect the Virgin Australia app within ChatGPT to enable functionality.

## How It Works

Users access the feature by:
1. Opening Apps in the ChatGPT sidebar
2. Searching for Virgin Australia
3. Connecting the app
4. Selecting "+" in chat and choosing Virgin Australia to begin planning

## Future Capabilities (In Development)

Planned features include searching partner airline flights, international routes (USA, UK, Europe, Asia, Middle East), day-of-travel flight details, and seat map insights.

## Leadership Commentary

CEO Dave Emerson stated the launch represents "a significant milestone" and emphasized: "we're giving our customers a faster, more intuitive way to plan and book their trips, all within a platform many are already using every day."

## Partnership Context

Virgin Australia collaborated with OpenAI on this integration, announced November 2025.

/home/nicholas-wood/Documents/workspace/personal/projects/career/artifacts/virgin-interview-prep/03-fastapi-and-fastmcp.md

CANDIDATE: Nicholas Wood, senior/lead software engineer, ~6.5 years. Primary stacks: Java/Spring (Macquarie, Leidos), Golang + gRPC/Protobuf (ANZ Plus, regulated banking, building generative-AI search APIs on Vertex AI/Gemini), TypeScript/React, plus a solo full-stack SaaS (AccessBuddy: Next.js, Postgres, Cloud Run, Stripe). He is strong on event-driven architecture, API design, TDD, and observability (OpenTelemetry). He has NOT used FastAPI in production but wants to confidently show he understands it. He knows REST/gRPC/HTTP deeply.

ROLE: Virgin Australia Senior AI Engineer (Brisbane, CIO/AI team). The position description explicitly lists "Python, FastAPI / FastMCP" as a required skill. Virgin has a live flight-search "app" inside ChatGPT (built on OpenAI's ChatGPT Apps platform, which is MCP-based) — so FastMCP is almost certainly how they expose flight-search tools to ChatGPT. Make this connection explicit.

INTERVIEW CONTEXT: Round 1 is conversational and high-level. NO coding challenge, NO leetcode. The interviewers ask a few very specific pointed questions to test depth, plus higher-level problem-solving. Using AI during the actual interview is an instant fail — so this is genuine learning. Nick must be able to explain every concept in his OWN WORDS, spoken aloud. Optimise for confident verbal articulation, not exhaustive reference. Jaimyn (the referrer) said they do NOT expect too much detail.

COVER (FastAPI): ASGI vs WSGI and why async matters; async/await route handlers and the sync-route threadpool trap; Pydantic models for request/response validation and serialisation; dependency injection via Depends; path/query/body params; response_model; automatic OpenAPI/Swagger docs; middleware; background tasks; startup/shutdown lifespan; auth (OAuth2 password flow, JWT bearer); error handling (HTTPException); Starlette/Uvicorn underpinnings and worker model; STREAMING responses / SSE (critical for LLM token streaming — connect to why this matters for AI apps); testing with TestClient/httpx; FastAPI vs Flask vs Django REST when-to-use. Frame FastAPI for someone who knows Spring Boot and Go: draw the analogies (Pydantic≈DTO validation, Depends≈DI container, decorators≈annotations).

COVER (FastMCP / MCP): what the Model Context Protocol is (open standard, originally from Anthropic, for connecting LLMs to external tools/data/prompts via a client-server model); the three MCP primitives (tools, resources, prompts); what FastMCP is (a Pythonic decorator-based framework for building MCP servers, deliberately FastAPI-like); transports (stdio for local, streamable HTTP/SSE for remote); how a remote MCP server becomes a "ChatGPT App"/connector; auth for remote MCP (OAuth); why an airline would build flight search as an MCP server (expose search_flights / get_reward_seats as tools the model calls). Give a tiny illustrative code sketch of a FastMCP tool.

FORMAT per topic:
1. Crisp mental model (2-4 sentences: what it is, why it exists)
2. The senior nuance — the trade-off, gotcha, or "thing that signals depth"
3. "If they ask..." — 2-5 likely pointed questions each with a strong, SPEAKABLE model answer in Nick's voice
4. Bridge to Nick — where his real Spring/Go/Next.js experience connects, so he answers from genuine ground

WRITING RULES: Australian English. NO em dashes (use commas, colons, or full stops). No AI-tell words (no "delve", "tapestry", "landscape", "it's not just X it's Y", "navigate the complexities"). Direct, dense, no filler openers. Answers must be speakable aloud. Start the file with a one-line title and a 2-sentence "how to use this doc". Aim for roughly 300-450 lines: thorough but not bloated. Do not flatter. Return only a 3-line summary of what you wrote (the file is the deliverable).

Write an interview-prep brushup document on React hooks and modern React fundamentals for a candidate. Write the file to:
/home/nicholas-wood/Documents/workspace/personal/projects/career/artifacts/virgin-interview-prep/04-react-hooks.md

CANDIDATE: Nicholas Wood, senior/lead software engineer, ~6.5 years. He has shipped React/TypeScript front-ends: a real-time asset-management portal at Macquarie (React), a Flash-to-modern-web rewrite at Leidos (Angular/TS, so he knows component frameworks), and his own solo SaaS AccessBuddy on Next.js (App Router, React Server Components, PWA with WebAuthn). So he is a capable but back-end-leaning engineer who needs to talk fluently about hooks, not learn them from scratch.

ROLE: Virgin Australia Senior AI Engineer (Brisbane, CIO/AI team). The PD lists "React + TypeScript" as a required skill. The AI team builds interfaces over AI systems, so front-end matters but the depth bar is "competent senior", not "front-end specialist".

INTERVIEW CONTEXT: Round 1 is conversational and high-level. NO coding challenge, NO leetcode. The interviewers (including an engineer named Harry and an engineering lead) ask a few very specific pointed questions to test depth in frontend JavaScript/React, plus higher-level problem-solving. Using AI during the actual interview is an instant fail — this is genuine learning. Nick must explain every concept in his OWN WORDS, spoken aloud. Optimise for confident verbal articulation. The referrer said they do NOT expect too much detail or for him to get everything right.

COVER: useState (and why state is immutable / functional updates); useEffect in depth (what it's for, the dependency array, cleanup functions, when effects run relative to render/paint, the stale-closure trap, infinite-loop pitfalls, and the modern "You Might Not Need an Effect" guidance — derived state, event handlers vs effects); useContext; useRef (DOM refs + mutable values that don't trigger render, useState vs useRef); useMemo and useCallback (memoisation, referential equality, when they actually help vs cargo-cult use, React.memo); useReducer (when over useState); custom hooks (extracting logic, naming convention); the Rules of Hooks and WHY they exist (call-order/linked-list mental model, no conditional hooks); controlled vs uncontrolled components; data-fetching: why useEffect-for-fetching is now discouraged and what replaced it (React Query/SWR, Server Components, Suspense); keys and reconciliation basics; concurrent features (useTransition, useDeferredValue, useId) at a high level; React Server Components vs Client Components and the "use client" boundary (relevant since AccessBuddy is Next.js App Router). 

FORMAT per topic:
1. Crisp mental model (2-4 sentences)
2. The senior nuance — the gotcha or the thing that signals depth (e.g. stale closures, referential equality, why hooks can't be conditional)
3. "If they ask..." — 2-5 likely pointed questions each with a strong, SPEAKABLE model answer in Nick's voice
4. Bridge to Nick — connect to his Macquarie React portal / Leidos rewrite / AccessBuddy Next.js work so he answers from real ground

Start with a one-line title and a 2-sentence "how to use this doc". Aim for roughly 300-450 lines: thorough but not bloated. Do not flatter. Return only a 3-line summary (the file is the deliverable).

input.prompt:
Write an interview-prep brushup document on senior-level Python fundamentals for a candidate. Write the file to:
/home/nicholas-wood/Documents/workspace/personal/projects/career/artifacts/virgin-interview-prep/05-senior-python.md

CANDIDATE: Nicholas Wood, senior/lead software engineer, ~6.5 years. His PRIMARY languages are Java (Spring Boot, at Macquarie and Leidos) and Golang (gRPC/Protobuf at ANZ Plus). He has used Python for data work and scripting and is comfortable in it, but it is not his deepest language. The most effective framing for him is "translate concepts you already know" — e.g. Go goroutines/channels vs Python asyncio, JVM threads vs the GIL, Java streams vs Python comprehensions/generators, Spring DI vs Python patterns. He needs to sound like a senior engineer who genuinely understands Python's model, not a tutorial reader.

ROLE: Virgin Australia Senior AI Engineer (Brisbane). The PD lists "Python" as the core language and the whole AI stack (FastAPI, RAG pipelines, evals, agents) is Python. Pointed questions will test whether he understands Python at depth, not just syntax.

INTERVIEW CONTEXT: Round 1 is conversational, high-level. NO coding challenge, NO leetcode. A few very specific pointed questions test depth, plus higher-level problem-solving. Using AI during the actual interview is an instant fail — genuine learning required. Nick must explain everything in his OWN WORDS, spoken aloud. Optimise for confident verbal articulation. The referrer said they do NOT expect too much detail or perfection.

COVER (senior depth, not beginner syntax): the data model and key dunder methods; mutable-default-argument gotcha (and why); list/dict/set comprehensions; iterators vs generators and yield (lazy evaluation, memory, when generators matter for data/RAG pipelines); decorators (how they work, functools.wraps, real uses); context managers (with, __enter__/__exit__, contextlib.contextmanager); type hints and the typing module (Optional, Union/|, generics, Protocol/structural typing, mypy, and that hints are not enforced at runtime); dataclasses vs Pydantic vs NamedTuple vs dict (and why Pydantic dominates in AI/FastAPI code); async/await and the asyncio event loop (coroutines, await, gather/TaskGroup, and crucially WHEN async helps — IO-bound vs CPU-bound); the GIL — explain it properly (what it protects, why it limits CPU-bound threading, threads vs multiprocessing vs async, and the 3.13+ free-threaded/no-GIL direction); packaging and environments (venv, pip, and the modern uv/poetry shift); testing with pytest (fixtures, parametrize, monkeypatch/mocking); exceptions and EAFP-vs-LBYL philosophy; where Python is slow and how people work around it (numpy vectorisation, C extensions, offloading to the model/DB); memory model (reference counting + cyclic GC). 

FORMAT per topic:
1. Crisp mental model (2-4 sentences)
2. The senior nuance — the gotcha or depth-signalling point
3. "If they ask..." — 2-5 likely pointed questions each with a strong, SPEAKABLE model answer in Nick's voice
4. Bridge from what Nick already knows — the Go/Java analogy so he reasons from his real strengths

Put EXTRA care into the GIL, generators, and async sections — these are the classic senior-Python depth probes.

WRITING RULES: Australian English. NO em dashes. No AI-tell words. Direct, dense, no filler. Answers speakable aloud. Start with a one-line title and a 2-sentence "how to use this doc". Aim for roughly 350-500 lines. Do not flatter. Return only a 3-line summary (the file is the deliverable).

# AI Systems Fundamentals — Virgin Senior AI Engineer

How to use this doc: this is the core of what Jaimyn told you to brush up on (RAG, safety, evals) plus the agentic and LLMOps material the PD leans on. Read it out loud. The goal is not to memorise definitions, it is to be able to explain each idea in your own words and then connect it to something you have actually built. Your ANZ Plus generative-AI search work is a real RAG system, so most of this you have lived, you just need the vocabulary tight.

Your single strongest move in this interview: when they ask about RAG, evals, or guardrails in the abstract, answer the concept cleanly in two sentences, then say "the way this showed up for me was..." and ground it in the ANZ Plus AI search platform. That converts a knowledge question into a credibility moment.

---

## 1. RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation)

### Mental model
RAG is giving a language model the right context at query time instead of relying on what is baked into its weights. You retrieve relevant documents from an external store, put them in the prompt, and ask the model to answer grounded in that material. It exists because models have a training cut-off, do not know your private data, and hallucinate when they answer from nothing.

### The pipeline (be able to draw this)
1. **Ingestion / indexing (offline):** take source documents, split them into chunks, run each chunk through an embedding model to get a vector, store the vector plus the original text and metadata in a vector store.
2. **Retrieval (at query time):** embed the user's query with the same model, do a similarity search (nearest neighbours) against the store, get the top-k chunks.
3. **Augmentation:** pack those chunks into the prompt as context, usually with the instruction "answer only from the provided context, and say you do not know if it is not there".
4. **Generation:** the model produces the answer grounded in the retrieved context, ideally with citations back to the source chunks.

### Senior nuance (this is where depth shows)
- **Retrieval quality is the whole game.** If retrieval returns the wrong chunks, no model can save you. Most "the LLM is wrong" complaints are actually retrieval failures. So you measure retrieval separately from generation.
- **Chunking strategy matters more than people expect.** Too big and you dilute relevance and waste context; too small and you lose the surrounding meaning. You chunk on semantic boundaries (sections, paragraphs) not arbitrary character counts, and you often add overlap so a fact split across a boundary is not lost.
- **Hybrid search beats pure vector search.** Dense vector search is good at meaning ("reward seat availability" matches "points redemption"), but bad at exact tokens (flight numbers, product codes, names). You combine it with keyword/BM25 (sparse) search and fuse the rankings. For an airline this is critical because users say exact route codes and dates.
- **Re-ranking.** Retrieve a wide net (say top 50) cheaply, then use a cross-encoder re-ranker to score query-document pairs properly and keep the best 5. First-stage retrieval is recall-oriented, re-ranking is precision-oriented.

### "Advanced RAG" (the PD literally lists this)
The PD says "Advanced RAG techniques (retrieval strategy, context packing, tool orchestration, safety/guardrails)". In your words:
- **Retrieval strategy:** hybrid search, re-ranking, metadata filtering (only search this customer's docs, only flights after this date), and query transformation (rewriting or expanding the user query, or breaking a multi-part question into sub-queries).
- **Context packing:** you have a finite context window and retrieved chunks compete for it. You order by relevance, deduplicate, sometimes compress or summarise chunks, and you put the most important material where the model attends best (start and end, the "lost in the middle" problem where models ignore the middle of long contexts).
- **Tool orchestration:** modern RAG is not always "retrieve once then answer". An agent can decide to search, look at results, search again with a refined query, or call a different tool (a live flight-availability API, not a document store). This is "agentic RAG".
- **Safety/guardrails:** see section 4.

### "If they ask..."
- **"What is RAG and why use it over fine-tuning?"** RAG injects knowledge at query time from an external store; fine-tuning bakes behaviour or style into the weights through more training. You reach for RAG when the knowledge is large, changes often, or needs to be auditable and citable, which is most enterprise knowledge. You fine-tune when you want to change how the model behaves, its format or tone, or to teach a narrow skill, not to teach it facts. They are not mutually exclusive. For something like flight data that changes by the minute you would not fine-tune at all, you would retrieve or call a live tool.
- **"How would you stop a RAG system hallucinating?"** Three layers. Ground it hard: instruct the model to answer only from retrieved context and to say it does not know otherwise. Make retrieval good so the context actually contains the answer. Then verify: cite sources so a human or a checker can trace claims back, and optionally run a faithfulness check that asks whether the answer is supported by the context. You cannot get to zero, so you also design the UX to show sources and set expectations.
- **"Your RAG answers are poor, how do you debug?"** Separate the stages. First check retrieval in isolation: for a failing query, are the right chunks even being returned in the top-k? If not, it is an indexing, chunking, embedding, or search problem, fix that first. If retrieval is good but the answer is bad, it is a generation/prompt problem. Most of the time it is retrieval.
- **"What is the embedding model's job?"** It maps text into a vector such that semantically similar text lands close together in that space. You must use the same embedding model for indexing and querying, and if you change the model you have to re-index everything.

### Bridge to Nick
This is your ANZ Plus work almost line for line. You "owned delivery of AI-enabled search APIs, a core component of a generative AI search platform leveraging Vertex AI / Gemini". Be ready to say: the platform let services surface answers from bank content, my piece was the search/retrieval API layer, and the engineering problem was exactly the one that matters in RAG, making retrieval good and the responses trustworthy in a regulated environment where a wrong answer has real consequences. You did this on Vertex AI, Virgin is on AWS/Databricks/pgvector, but the architecture is identical, only the managed services differ.

---

## 2. Embeddings and vector databases

### Mental model
An embedding is a list of numbers (a vector, often 768 or 1536 dimensions) that represents the meaning of a piece of text. Similar meanings produce vectors that are close together, measured usually by cosine similarity. A vector database stores these and answers "find me the k nearest vectors to this one" fast, even over millions of items.

### Senior nuance
- **Approximate nearest neighbour (ANN).** Exact nearest-neighbour over millions of vectors is too slow, so vector DBs use ANN indexes (HNSW is the common one, a navigable graph) that trade a tiny bit of recall for a massive speed-up. Knowing the name HNSW and that it is a graph-based index signals depth.
- **pgvector (the PD lists it):** it is a Postgres extension that adds a vector column type and similarity search. The advantage is you keep your vectors next to your relational data and operational tooling, one database, transactional, familiar. The trade-off versus a dedicated vector DB (Pinecone, Weaviate) is scale and some specialised features, but for a lot of enterprise workloads pgvector is the pragmatic right answer. You can speak to this credibly because AccessBuddy runs on Postgres.
- **Metadata filtering.** Real systems do not just do pure vector search, they filter, only this tenant, only documents newer than X. Doing the filter and the vector search efficiently together is a real engineering concern.

### "If they ask..."
- **"Cosine similarity vs Euclidean distance?"** Cosine measures the angle between vectors, so it cares about direction/meaning not magnitude, which is what you want for text embeddings. It is the default for semantic search.
- **"How big should a chunk be?"** It depends on the content and the embedding model's context limit, but the principle is one coherent idea per chunk with a little overlap. You tune it empirically against your eval set rather than guessing.

### Bridge to Nick
You run Postgres in production on AccessBuddy and you have built search before at Leidos (a data discovery platform that "reduced analyst discovery tasks from months to seconds", integrating multiple sources into a central searchable system). That Leidos system is a great non-LLM retrieval story, you understand the indexing and relevance problem from first principles, RAG just adds the embedding and generation layers.

---

## 3. Agents, tool/function calling, planning, memory

### Mental model
An agent is an LLM in a loop that can take actions, not just produce text. You give the model a set of tools (functions it can call), it decides which to call and with what arguments, you execute the call and feed the result back, and it continues until it can answer. "Function calling" or "tool calling" is the mechanism: the model outputs a structured request (tool name plus JSON arguments) instead of prose, your code runs the real function, and returns the result.

### The loop (be able to describe it)
1. User asks something.
2. Model decides: answer directly, or call a tool. It emits a structured tool call.
3. Your runtime executes the tool (an API call, a DB query, a search) and returns the result.
4. Model sees the result and either calls another tool or produces the final answer.
This is the ReAct pattern at heart: reason, act, observe, repeat.

### The three things the PD names: prompting, function/tool use, planning, memory
- **Tool use:** as above. The key engineering point is you define tools with clear schemas and descriptions, because the model chooses tools based on those descriptions. Bad tool descriptions cause bad tool selection.
- **Planning:** for multi-step tasks the agent breaks the goal into steps. Simple version is the model plans implicitly each turn; more structured version uses an explicit plan-then-execute approach, or a graph of steps (this is what LangGraph gives you, a state machine of nodes and edges so the flow is controllable and debuggable rather than a free-running loop).
- **Memory:** short-term memory is the conversation context window. Long-term memory is storing facts/preferences/history outside the window and retrieving them when relevant, which is itself a RAG problem. "What did this customer book last time" is a memory retrieval, not a context-window thing.

### Senior nuance
- **Agents are powerful and unreliable, so you constrain them.** The more free-running the loop, the more ways it fails (wrong tool, infinite loops, compounding errors). Senior framing: prefer the most constrained design that solves the problem. A fixed pipeline or a controllable graph beats an open-ended agent when you can get away with it. You add autonomy only where the task genuinely needs it.
- **Determinism and guardrails around tools.** Tools that change state (book a flight, charge a card) need confirmation steps, idempotency, and human-in-the-loop gates. The model can be wrong, so the action layer must be safe by construction. This is exactly the "human-in-the-loop controls" the PD mentions under AgentOps.
- **Structured output.** Function calling is also how you get reliable structured data out of a model, you define a schema and the model fills it. This is the same primitive whether you are calling a tool or just extracting fields.

### "If they ask..."
- **"What is function calling?"** The model is given tool definitions with JSON schemas. Instead of answering in prose, it can emit a structured call naming a tool and its arguments. My code executes the real function and returns the result, the model continues. It is how you connect a model to live systems like a flight search API.
- **"When would you NOT use an agent?"** When a deterministic pipeline does the job. Agents add latency, cost, and failure modes. If the task is "retrieve and answer" you do not need an autonomous loop. I reach for agents when the path genuinely varies per request and the model needs to decide the steps.
- **"How do you stop an agent doing something dangerous?"** Constrain the tools it has, require confirmation and human approval for state-changing actions, make those actions idempotent, put hard limits on loop iterations and spend, and log every tool call for audit. You design so the worst a wrong decision can do is bounded.

### Bridge to Nick
At ANZ you "drove AI integration strategy, making decisions on model selection, provisioning approach, and scaling patterns" and "established practical guardrails for generative AI use, balancing capability with compliance". That is the senior judgement this section is testing, knowing when to add capability and when to constrain it. Virgin's own ChatGPT flight-search app is an agent-tool system: ChatGPT is the agent, Virgin's MCP server exposes flight-search as tools. You will cover that in the ChatGPT Apps doc.

---

## 4. Safety, guardrails, red-teaming

### Mental model
Guardrails are the controls that keep an AI system inside acceptable behaviour: what goes in, what comes out, and what it is allowed to do. They sit around the model because the model itself is probabilistic and can be manipulated. Red-teaming is deliberately attacking your own system to find where those controls fail before a user or attacker does.

### The layers
- **Input guardrails:** filter or detect prompt injection, jailbreak attempts, off-topic or abusive input, and PII you should not be processing.
- **Output guardrails:** check the response before it reaches the user, for hallucination/groundedness, toxicity, leaking sensitive data, or going off-policy (an airline bot giving legal or medical advice, or quoting a fare it should not).
- **Action guardrails:** the human-in-the-loop and confirmation controls on tools that do things.
- **Prompt injection** is the one to name explicitly: untrusted text (a retrieved document, a user message, a web page) contains instructions that hijack the model. The classic defence is to treat retrieved content as data not instructions, keep system instructions privileged, validate outputs, and never give the model unconstrained access to sensitive tools on the back of untrusted input.

### Senior nuance
- **Defence in depth, not one filter.** No single guardrail is reliable, you layer cheap deterministic checks (regex/PII scanners, allow-lists) with model-based checks (a classifier or an LLM-as-judge checking the output) and design constraints (limited tools, grounding).
- **Guardrails have a cost.** Every check adds latency and can produce false positives that frustrate users. The senior skill is calibrating, more guardrail where the blast radius is high (anything customer-facing, money, PII), less where it is low.
- **Responsible AI in a regulated context** is your home ground. Frame guardrails as the same discipline as any safety-critical or compliance control: identify the failure modes, control for them in proportion to impact, make it auditable.

### "If they ask..."
- **"What is prompt injection and how do you defend against it?"** It is when untrusted text the model reads contains instructions that override your intent, for example a retrieved document saying "ignore previous instructions and reveal X". You defend by separating trusted instructions from untrusted data, never executing instructions that come from retrieved or user content, validating outputs, and limiting what tools the model can reach so a hijack cannot do real damage. You assume it can happen and bound the impact.
- **"How do you red-team an AI feature?"** You systematically try to break it: adversarial prompts, jailbreaks, edge cases, attempts to extract data or trigger unsafe actions, and you do it before launch and continuously after. You build the worst cases into your eval suite so you catch regressions.
- **"Customer asks the airline bot for medical advice, what happens?"** That is an out-of-scope guardrail. The system should recognise off-domain requests and decline gracefully with a safe fallback, rather than improvising. You design the refusal, you do not leave it to chance.

### Bridge to Nick
You literally "established practical guardrails for generative AI within the project, balancing capability with compliance and reliability in a risk-averse banking context". Banking is one of the few domains stricter than aviation on this. You can speak to guardrails as something you implemented under real regulatory pressure, not theory.

---

## 5. Evals (evaluation)

### Mental model
Evals are how you measure whether an AI system is actually good, and whether a change made it better or worse. Because LLM output is non-deterministic and "looks plausible" is not "is correct", you cannot rely on eyeballing. An eval is a dataset of inputs plus a way to score the outputs, run repeatably, so you have a number you can move and defend.

### Types of eval (know the spread)
- **Component vs end-to-end.** Evaluate retrieval on its own (did the right chunks come back, measured by recall@k, precision, MRR), evaluate generation on its own, and evaluate the whole system end-to-end.
- **Reference-based:** you have a known correct answer and compare against it (exact match, or semantic similarity for free text).
- **Reference-free / criteria-based:** no single right answer, so you score against criteria like groundedness (is the answer supported by the context), relevance, helpfulness, tone.
- **LLM-as-judge:** use a strong model to score outputs against a rubric. Scales far better than human review, but you have to validate the judge against human labels and watch its biases (it favours longer answers, its own style, position).
- **Human eval:** the gold standard for the hard cases, expensive, so you use it to calibrate the automated evals and to spot-check.
- **Online vs offline.** Offline is against a fixed dataset in CI before you ship. Online is in production: A/B tests, user feedback (thumbs up/down), and operational metrics.

### Senior nuance
- **Evals are a dataset problem first.** The hard part is building a representative, versioned eval set that covers the real distribution including the nasty edge cases. A good eval set is an asset you grow over time, every production failure becomes a new test case.
- **Evals belong in CI/CD.** The PD calls for "automated evals" and "canary/shadow". The mature pattern: a prompt or model or retrieval change must pass the eval suite before it ships, the same way code must pass tests. This is the bit most teams are immature on and where your TDD-and-coverage discipline transfers directly.
- **You cannot optimise what you cannot measure.** Every prompt tweak feels like an improvement until you have a number. Evals are what turn "vibes-based" prompt engineering into engineering.

### "If they ask..."
- **"How do you know your RAG system is good?"** I measure it, not eyeball it. I separate retrieval metrics (recall@k, is the right context being found) from answer metrics (groundedness and correctness, often via an LLM-judge validated against human labels), I run them on a versioned eval set in CI, and I track online signals like user feedback and A/B results in production. Every failure I see becomes a new case in the set.
- **"What is LLM-as-judge and what is the risk?"** Using a strong model to grade outputs against a rubric so evaluation scales. The risks are the judge having biases, favouring verbosity, its own phrasing, the first option, and drifting, so you validate it against human ratings and keep humans in the loop on the hard slices.
- **"How do you test something non-deterministic?"** You shift from exact assertions to distributional and criteria-based checks: run a representative set, score against criteria, and assert on aggregate quality and on specific must-pass cases rather than one exact string. You also pin what you can (temperature 0 for tests where you want determinism).

### Bridge to Nick
You "established and enforced 80%+ test coverage with TDD across services" at ANZ and "defined engineering standards including TDD" at Macquarie. Evals are TDD for AI. Your strongest framing for the whole interview: most teams can get a demo working, the senior engineering is in testing, evaluation, and observability, which is exactly what the PD says Virgin values ("recognising the realities of delivery... production-ready solutions, including testing, evaluation and observability"). That sentence in the PD is aimed straight at people like you.

---

## 6. LLMOps / AgentOps and observability

### Mental model
LLMOps is MLOps for LLM systems: the operational discipline of running these things in production reliably. It covers prompt and config management (versioning prompts like code), the eval pipeline in CI, model/version registries, safe rollout (canary, shadow, feature flags, A/B), monitoring, and incident response. AgentOps is the same applied to agent systems specifically, with extra attention on tracing multi-step tool calls.

### What to be able to talk about
- **Prompt/config management:** prompts are not constants buried in code, they are versioned, reviewed, and tied to eval runs, so you can roll a prompt back like a deploy.
- **Observability for LLMs:** beyond normal metrics/logs/traces, you trace the full chain of a request, the retrieved chunks, the prompt sent, the tool calls, the tokens, the latency and cost per call. Tools like LangSmith, Langfuse, or Arize do this; the concept is the same tracing discipline as OpenTelemetry, which you already do, applied to the AI pipeline. You capture token usage and cost as first-class metrics because they drive both the bill and latency.
- **Rollout:** canary (release to a small slice first), shadow (run the new system alongside the old on real traffic without showing users, compare), feature flags (turn it on/off without redeploying), A/B (measure one variant against another). These let you ship AI changes safely despite non-determinism. This is the PD's "canary/A-B experiments, feature flags and controlled exposure".
- **Feedback loops:** capture user feedback and failures, feed them back into the eval set and the next iteration.

### Senior nuance
- **The metrics that matter are quality, latency, cost, and safety, together.** A change that improves answer quality but doubles latency or cost might be a net loss. You watch them as a set.
- **Non-determinism makes monitoring different.** You cannot alert on "output changed". You monitor distributions, quality scores on sampled traffic, refusal rates, retrieval hit rates, and user feedback trends, and you alert on drift.

### "If they ask..."
- **"How do you safely roll out a change to a live AI feature?"** Behind a feature flag, to a canary slice first, ideally shadow-tested against the current system on real traffic so I can compare quality before exposing users, with the eval suite passed in CI as the gate. I watch quality, latency, cost, and safety signals, and I can roll back instantly because the prompt and config are versioned.
- **"What do you monitor in production for an LLM app?"** The usual reliability signals plus AI-specific ones: per-request traces of retrieval and tool calls, token usage and cost, latency, quality scores on sampled outputs, refusal and error rates, and user feedback. I trace end to end so when something goes wrong I can see which stage failed.

### Bridge to Nick
OpenTelemetry instrumentation and production observability are in every one of your roles. You "instrumented distributed tracing and production observability via OpenTelemetry" at ANZ and Macquarie, and ran AccessBuddy on OpenTelemetry, Sentry, and Better Stack. LLMOps observability is the same instinct extended to the AI pipeline. You are not learning a new discipline, you are applying one you already own to a new layer.

---

## 7. The 90-second "AI systems" headline (rehearse this)

If they open with "talk me through your AI experience" or "what do you know about building AI systems", lead with this shape, then expand on whichever beat they pull:

"At ANZ Plus I owned the search APIs inside a generative-AI search platform on Vertex AI and Gemini, in a regulated banking environment. So I have built the retrieval side of a real RAG system, made decisions on model selection and scaling, and put practical guardrails around generative AI where a wrong or non-compliant answer actually matters. The pattern I care about most is that getting a demo working is easy, the engineering is in retrieval quality, evaluation, guardrails, and observability, treating AI systems with the same testing and operational rigour as any production system. That is the same TDD-and-observability discipline I have run across banking and asset management, just applied to the AI layer."

That hits RAG, model selection, guardrails, evals, observability, and regulated-context judgement in four sentences, every one backed by something you actually did.
