25	Run any enhancement through these eight beats. This doubles as your answer structure for any "how would you build X" system-design question in the interview, LIMSOC or otherwise.
26	
27	1. **Problem and users.** What real pain, for whom, and what does success look like operationally. Resist starting with the tech.
28	2. **Why AI, honestly.** What specifically needs a model versus deterministic software. Staff-level engineers are quick to say "this part does not need AI". 
29	3. **Data paths.** Sources, ingestion, where knowledge lives, retrieval vs live tools, data quality, and crucially PII and sensitivity (incident data is sensitive, just like member banking data).
30	4. **The AI design.** RAG, tools/agents, model choice, prompt and context strategy. Justify each. Name when you would not use RAG (volatile or exact data, use live tools).
31	5. **Guardrails and safety.** Failure modes, human-in-the-loop, what the system is never allowed to decide alone. In an emergency context this is the heart of it: AI assists, humans decide.
32	6. **Evals.** How you measure it is good, the dataset, component vs end-to-end, online signals, and the must-pass safety cases.
33	7. **Rollout and ops.** Canary, shadow, feature flags, observability, and the federated rollout reality across jurisdictions.
34	8. **Trade-offs and what is out of scope.** Where you compromised and why, what you deliberately left out, and the risks you are accepting.
35	
36	## 4. Worked example (placeholder - replace with your real proposal)
37	
38	> This is my plausible reconstruction so you can see the shape. It is probably adjacent to what you actually proposed. Tell me your real enhancements and I will redo this as yours.
39	
40	### Enhancement: incident decision-support assistant
41	**Problem and users.** During an incident, a communications operator or coordinator has to pull together the right information (SOPs, the relevant escalation pathway, who is on call, similar past incidents) and reach the right people fast, under time pressure. Latency and missed context cost outcomes. Users are operators and coordinators in the moment, not analysts after the fact.
42	
43	**Why AI.** The retrieval and synthesis is where a model helps: turning a messy, fast-evolving situation into "here is the relevant SOP, here is the escalation path, here are the people to notify, here is what a similar incident did". The decision and the action stay human. Dispatch logic and notifications themselves are deterministic software, not AI.
44	
45	**Data paths.** RAG over SOPs, escalation matrices, and policy (slow-changing, perfect for retrieval, with citations so an operator can trust and verify). Live tools for volatile data: who is currently on call, current resourcing, current conditions, these you call live, you do not embed them. Incident data is sensitive, so access is scoped and audited, same PII discipline as banking.
46	
47	**AI design.** Hybrid: RAG for the knowledge, tool-calling for live state. A constrained assistant, not a free-running agent, because this is safety-critical, the flow should be controllable and inspectable (a graph of steps, not an open loop). Model choice balances latency (operators need it now) against capability, and runs where the data governance allows.
48	
49	**Guardrails and safety.** The non-negotiable: the system suggests, humans decide and act. Every suggestion is grounded and cited so it can be checked. It declines or flags uncertainty rather than guessing. It can never trigger a notification or dispatch on its own, those stay human-confirmed and idempotent. Off-domain or low-confidence cases fail safe to "escalate to a human".
50	
51	**Evals.** A versioned set of real (de-identified) incident scenarios with expert-validated "right information / right people" answers. Component evals on retrieval (did it surface the correct SOP and pathway, recall@k) and on tool calls (right on-call lookup). End-to-end eval on whether the synthesised support matches what an experienced coordinator would want. Must-pass safety cases that never regress. Online: operator feedback and post-incident review feeding new cases back in.
52	
53	**Rollout and ops.** Shadow first, run it alongside live operations without operators acting on it, and compare its suggestions to what experienced coordinators actually did, before it is ever in the loop. Then canary to one jurisdiction or one operator cohort, feature-flagged, with full tracing of retrievals and tool calls. Federated rollout respects that jurisdictions differ in readiness, so it is staged, not switched on nationally at once.
54	
55	**Trade-offs and out of scope.** Out of scope at launch: any autonomous action, that is deliberately off the table in a safety-critical first version. Trade-off: more guardrail and human-confirmation means more friction and latency, accepted because the cost of a wrong autonomous action in an emergency is unacceptable. Risk accepted: it depends on SOP data quality, so data curation is part of the work, not an afterthought.

1	# FastAPI and FastMCP Fundamentals: Interview Brushup
2	
3	This is a confidence-and-articulation doc, not a reference manual: read each topic's mental model and the "speakable" answers out loud until you can say them in your own words without notes. You know REST, gRPC, HTTP, DI, and async deeply already, so most of this is mapping concepts you own onto Python names, not learning new ideas.
4	
5	## How FastAPI and FastMCP connect to the Virgin role
6	
7	Virgin's CIO/AI team runs a live flight-search experience inside ChatGPT, built on OpenAI's ChatGPT Apps platform. ChatGPT Apps are MCP-based: the app is a remote MCP server that exposes tools (like flight search) which the model calls on the user's behalf. FastMCP is the Pythonic framework for building those MCP servers, and it is deliberately shaped like FastAPI. So the stack is almost certainly: FastAPI for normal HTTP/AI service endpoints, FastMCP for the tools ChatGPT calls, both async, both Pydantic-typed. If you can talk about FastAPI's async model and Pydantic, FastMCP follows naturally, because it reuses the same mental furniture.
8	
9	The one-sentence version to have ready: "FastAPI is the async Python web framework for building the AI service APIs, and FastMCP is the same idea applied to MCP, so the flight-search tools Virgin exposes to ChatGPT are almost certainly FastMCP tools."
10	
11	---
12	
13	# PART 1: FastAPI
14	
15	## ASGI vs WSGI, and why async matters
16	
17	**Mental model.** WSGI is the old synchronous Python web standard: one worker handles one request at a time, blocking until it finishes. ASGI is the async successor: a single worker can hold thousands of in-flight requests, suspending each one while it waits on I/O and doing other work in the meantime. FastAPI is built on ASGI, which is what lets it handle high-concurrency I/O-bound workloads (calling an LLM, hitting a database, fanning out to other services) on a small number of workers.
18	
19	**Senior nuance.** Async only helps when you are I/O-bound, not CPU-bound. The whole point is the event loop reclaims the thread while you wait on the network. If you do heavy CPU work inside an async handler, you block the event loop and stall every other concurrent request on that worker. For AI workloads this matters enormously: an LLM call can take many seconds, and during that wait one async worker can serve hundreds of other requests instead of sitting idle.
20	
21	**If they ask...**
22	
23	- *"Why is FastAPI async, and when does that actually help?"*
24	  "Because it is built on ASGI rather than the old synchronous WSGI standard. The benefit is concurrency on I/O-bound work. When a handler is waiting on a slow network call, the event loop frees the thread to serve other requests instead of blocking. For AI services that is the dominant case: you spend most of your time waiting on an LLM or a database, so a few async workers can hold a lot of concurrent requests. It does not speed up CPU-bound work, it just stops you wasting threads on waiting."
25	
26	- *"What happens if you do something slow and synchronous inside an async route?"*
27	  "You block the event loop. The whole worker stops servicing other requests until that blocking call returns, so your concurrency collapses. The fix is either make it genuinely async, or push it off the event loop, for example onto a thread pool or a background worker."
28	
29	**Bridge to Nick.** This is the same reasoning you already apply in Go. Go's goroutines and async I/O exist for exactly this: don't block a thread waiting on the network. ASGI is Python catching up to what Go gave you natively. When you talk about it, you can frame it as "this is the goroutine intuition, just expressed through an event loop instead of the runtime scheduler."
30	
31	## async/await handlers and the sync-route threadpool trap
32	
33	**Mental model.** In FastAPI you write a route as either `async def` or plain `def`. An `async def` route runs directly on the event loop, so you must only `await` non-blocking things inside it. A plain `def` route is the escape hatch: FastAPI runs it in a thread pool so a blocking call inside it does not freeze the loop.
34	
35	**Senior nuance.** The trap is mixing them up. If you write `async def` but then call a blocking, synchronous library inside it (a sync database driver, `requests`, `time.sleep`), you block the event loop and silently kill concurrency. The counterintuitive rule: if your dependency is blocking and you have no async version, a plain `def` route is safer than an `async def` one, because FastAPI offloads the `def` route to a thread. People assume `async` is always faster and reach for it reflexively, which is the actual footgun.
36	
37	**If they ask...**
38	
39	- *"When would you use a normal `def` route instead of `async def`?"*
40	  "When the work inside is blocking and I have no async-native library for it. FastAPI runs plain `def` routes in a thread pool, so a blocking call there doesn't stall the event loop. If I forced it into an `async def` and called the blocking thing directly, I would freeze the loop. So `async def` for genuinely async work, plain `def` for blocking work I can't make async."
41	
42	- *"Common async mistake you have seen?"*
43	  "Writing `async def` and then calling a synchronous client inside it, like a blocking HTTP library. It looks async, it passes tests, and under load the throughput is terrible because every one of those calls blocks the loop. The tell is that concurrency doesn't scale even though everything says async."
44	
45	**Bridge to Nick.** In Spring you mostly think per-request-thread (servlet model), so blocking is fine because each request has its own thread. FastAPI's `def` route in a thread pool is essentially that Spring model on demand, while `async def` is the new event-loop model. You can say: "the plain `def` route gives me the per-thread Spring behaviour when I need it, and `async def` is for the event-loop path."
46	
47	## Pydantic models for request/response validation and serialisation
48	
49	**Mental model.** Pydantic is the typed data layer. You declare a class with typed fields, and FastAPI uses it to validate and parse the incoming JSON body automatically, rejecting bad input with a structured 422 error before your code runs. The same models serialise your responses back to JSON. It is schema-as-code: the type annotations are the contract.
50	
51	**Senior nuance.** Pydantic isn't just validation, it is the single source of truth that also generates the OpenAPI schema and the docs. One model definition gives you parsing, validation, serialisation, editor autocompletion, and API documentation. The depth signal is knowing the boundary discipline: you validate and coerce at the edge of the system, so everything inside your handler is already a typed, trusted object, never a raw dict.
52	
53	**If they ask...**
54	
55	- *"What does Pydantic give you?"*
56	  "Typed request and response models. I declare a class with typed fields, and FastAPI validates the incoming JSON against it automatically. Bad input gets rejected with a structured error before my handler runs, and the same model serialises the response. The nice part is one definition drives validation, serialisation, and the OpenAPI schema, so the types are the contract."
57	
58	- *"How is that different from just parsing a dict?"*
59	  "With a dict, every field access is an assumption that could be wrong at runtime, and validation is scattered. With Pydantic the validation happens once at the boundary, and inside the handler I'm working with a typed object I can trust. It moves the failure to the edge where it belongs and gives me an explicit, documented contract."
60	
61	**Bridge to Nick.** This is DTO validation, the same pattern as Bean Validation / `@Valid` on a request DTO in Spring, or a typed struct with validation in Go. Frame it directly: "Pydantic is DTO validation. It's the `@Valid` annotated request DTO from Spring, except the type annotations also generate the OpenAPI schema for free." That instantly shows you understand it as a known pattern, not a novelty.
62	
63	## Dependency injection via Depends
64	
65	**Mental model.** FastAPI's `Depends` is its dependency injection mechanism. You declare a dependency (a function that produces something, like a database session, the current user, or a config object) and FastAPI resolves it and injects the result into your handler. Dependencies can depend on other dependencies, and FastAPI caches and wires the whole graph per request.
66	
67	**Senior nuance.** Depends is how you do cross-cutting concerns cleanly: auth, database sessions, pagination params, rate-limit checks. The elegant bit is that a dependency can `yield`, which lets it run setup before the request and teardown after (open a DB session, yield it, close it on the way out), so it doubles as scoped resource management. The depth point: this is constructor injection done per-request, and it keeps handlers thin and testable because you can override any dependency in tests.
68	
69	**If they ask...**
70	
71	- *"How does dependency injection work in FastAPI?"*
72	  "Through `Depends`. I write a function that produces a dependency, like a database session or the authenticated user, and declare it as a parameter on the route. FastAPI resolves the dependency graph per request and injects the results. Dependencies can depend on each other, and one that uses `yield` can do setup and teardown around the request, so it handles scoped resources like a DB session cleanly."
73	
74	- *"Why is that useful for testing?"*
75	  "Because I can override any dependency. In a test I swap the real database dependency for a fake or an in-memory one without touching the handler. The handler just declares what it needs, so I control what gets injected. It keeps the handler thin and the wiring explicit."
76	
77	**Bridge to Nick.** This is the DI container you already know from Spring, just request-scoped and function-based instead of annotation-and-bean-based. Say it plainly: "`Depends` is the DI container. It is Spring's `@Autowired` and bean wiring, but resolved per request as a function graph, and the `yield` form is basically a scoped bean with a destroy method." Spring engineers immediately get this.
78	
79	## Path, query, and body params
80	
81	**Mental model.** FastAPI infers where each parameter comes from by its type and declaration. A parameter named in the route path (like `/flights/{id}`) is a path param. A simple scalar not in the path becomes a query param. A Pydantic model parameter is read from the request body. You rarely have to say which is which; the function signature declares the whole input contract.
82	
83	**Senior nuance.** Because the parameter types drive parsing, validation, and the OpenAPI schema all at once, your function signature is the API spec. You can add constraints inline (a query param with a max length, an integer with a minimum) and those become both runtime validation and documented schema. The signal is understanding that there is no separate "parse the request" step; the typed signature is the parsing layer.
84	
85	**If they ask...**
86	
87	- *"How does FastAPI know if something is a path, query, or body parameter?"*
88	  "From the function signature. If the name appears in the route path it's a path param. A plain scalar that isn't in the path becomes a query param. A Pydantic model parameter is read from the request body. So the signature itself declares the full input contract, and the same declaration drives validation and the docs."
89	
90	**Bridge to Nick.** In Spring this is `@PathVariable`, `@RequestParam`, `@RequestBody`; in Go with gRPC the request message is the typed contract. FastAPI collapses all three into the typed signature. Frame: "It's `@PathVariable` / `@RequestParam` / `@RequestBody` inferred from types instead of annotations."
91	
92	## response_model and automatic OpenAPI/Swagger docs
93	
94	**Mental model.** `response_model` declares the Pydantic type of what a route returns. FastAPI uses it to serialise the response, and crucially to filter it: anything not in the response model is stripped out, so you can return a rich internal object and only expose the declared fields. Separately, FastAPI generates an OpenAPI schema from all your types and serves interactive Swagger UI and ReDoc docs automatically, with zero extra code.
95	
96	**Senior nuance.** `response_model` is a security and contract tool, not just serialisation. Declaring an output model means you cannot accidentally leak internal fields (a password hash, an internal flag) even if your handler returns an object that has them, because the response model defines the allow-list. The depth signal: input and output models are deliberately different types, so the shape you accept is decoupled from the shape you return.
97	
98	**If they ask...**
99	
100	- *"What does response_model do, beyond serialisation?"*
101	  "It defines the output contract and acts as an allow-list. FastAPI filters the response down to exactly the fields in the model, so even if my handler returns an object carrying extra internal fields, only the declared ones go out. That stops accidental data leaks, and it documents the response shape in OpenAPI. I usually keep the input and output models separate so the accepted shape and the returned shape are independent."
102	
103	- *"Where do the API docs come from?"*
104	  "They're generated from the types. FastAPI builds an OpenAPI schema from the path, query, body, and response models, and serves interactive Swagger UI and ReDoc automatically. I don't write the spec by hand; the typed code is the spec."
105	
106	**Bridge to Nick.** You know OpenAPI/Swagger well and you have done API-first design. The pitch: "I've done API-first and OpenAPI work; FastAPI inverts it to code-first but the spec is always accurate because it's generated from the same types that do validation. `response_model` is the response DTO with field projection, which also gives me leak protection by default."
107	
108	## Middleware
109	
110	**Mental model.** Middleware wraps every request and response, running code before the handler and after it. You use it for cross-cutting concerns that apply globally: logging, request timing, adding headers, CORS, correlation IDs, catching and shaping errors. It sits in the request pipeline around your routes.
111	
112	**Senior nuance.** The distinction worth knowing: middleware is for truly global, per-request concerns; `Depends` is for per-route, injectable concerns. Use middleware for things like attaching a trace ID to every request and logging latency; use Depends for auth and resource scoping that vary by route. Reaching for middleware when you meant a dependency (or vice versa) is the common design smell.
113	
114	**If they ask...**
115	
116	- *"Middleware versus a dependency, when do you use which?"*
117	  "Middleware for global, per-request concerns that wrap everything: request logging, timing, CORS, attaching a correlation ID. Dependencies for per-route concerns I want injected and testable: auth, a DB session, pagination. If it applies to every request uniformly and doesn't need to be injected into the handler, it's middleware; if a specific route needs it as a value, it's a dependency."
118	
119	**Bridge to Nick.** This is servlet filters / Spring interceptors, or Go HTTP middleware chains. You have built observability with OpenTelemetry, so frame it: "Middleware is where I'd wire request-level OpenTelemetry spans and correlation IDs, same place I'd put a filter in Spring or a middleware in a Go handler chain."
120	
121	## Background tasks
122	
123	**Mental model.** A background task lets a handler schedule work to run after the response is sent. The client gets its response immediately, and FastAPI runs the task afterwards in the same process. Typical uses: send a confirmation email, write an audit log, invalidate a cache, things the caller doesn't need to wait for.
124	
125	**Senior nuance.** Background tasks run in-process and are fire-and-forget with no durability. If the process dies, the task is lost; there is no retry, no persistence. So they are right for low-stakes, best-effort follow-ups, and wrong for anything that must not be lost, which belongs on a real queue or worker (Celery, a Pub/Sub consumer, etc.). Knowing that boundary is the senior signal.
126	
127	**If they ask...**
128	
129	- *"When would you use a background task, and when not?"*
130	  "I use them for cheap, best-effort work the client shouldn't wait on, like firing off an email or writing an audit entry after the response goes out. I wouldn't use them for anything that must not be lost, because they run in-process with no durability or retry. If the work is critical, it goes on a proper queue or worker instead."
131	
132	**Bridge to Nick.** You are strong on event-driven architecture, so the contrast is natural: "Background tasks are the lightweight in-process option. For anything durable I'd publish an event to Pub/Sub and have a consumer handle it, same as the event-driven patterns I built at ANZ."
133	
134	## Startup/shutdown lifespan
135	
136	**Mental model.** The lifespan handler runs code once when the app starts and once when it shuts down. You use it to set up and tear down shared resources: open a database connection pool, initialise an HTTP client or an LLM client, load a model into memory on startup, and close all of it cleanly on shutdown.
137	
138	**Senior nuance.** The modern API is a single `lifespan` async context manager (setup before `yield`, teardown after), which replaced the older separate startup/shutdown event handlers. The reason it matters for AI services: you want to create the LLM client, connection pool, or load a model once at boot and reuse it across requests, not per-request. Per-request setup of an expensive client is a classic performance bug.
139	
140	**If they ask...**
141	
142	- *"How do you manage shared resources like a connection pool or an LLM client?"*
143	  "Through the lifespan handler. It runs once at startup and once at shutdown, so I open the connection pool or initialise the LLM client there, hold it for the app's lifetime, and close it cleanly on shutdown. The mistake to avoid is creating an expensive client per request; lifespan is where you do it once and reuse it."
144	
145	**Bridge to Nick.** This is `@PostConstruct`/`@PreDestroy` or Spring bean lifecycle, or `main()` setup and deferred cleanup in Go. "Lifespan is the app lifecycle hook: it's where the connection pool and clients get built once, same as bean init in Spring or setup-and-defer in a Go main."
146	
147	## Auth: OAuth2 password flow and JWT bearer
148	
149	**Mental model.** FastAPI ships OAuth2 helpers. The password flow takes a username and password at a token endpoint and issues a token, typically a JWT. On every subsequent request the client sends that JWT as a bearer token in the Authorization header. A dependency validates the token (checks signature and expiry, decodes the claims) and injects the current user, so any route can require auth just by depending on it.
150	
151	**Senior nuance.** JWTs are stateless and self-contained, which is the strength and the trap. The server can verify a JWT without a database lookup because the signature proves it is valid, but that also means you cannot easily revoke one before it expires. So you keep token lifetimes short and use refresh tokens for longer sessions. Knowing the revocation trade-off is the depth signal; lots of people can wire JWT auth but fewer can articulate why short expiries and refresh tokens exist.
152	
153	**If they ask...**
154	
155	- *"How does auth work in FastAPI?"*
156	  "FastAPI has OAuth2 helpers. A token endpoint takes credentials and issues a JWT, and the client sends it as a bearer token on later requests. I validate the token in a dependency: check the signature and expiry, decode the claims, and inject the current user. Then any protected route just depends on that, so auth is declarative per route."
157	
158	- *"What's the downside of JWTs?"*
159	  "They're stateless, so I can verify them without a database hit, but I also can't easily revoke one before it expires, because validity is just the signature. So I keep access tokens short-lived and use refresh tokens for longer sessions. If I genuinely need instant revocation I'd need a denylist or a stateful session, which gives back some of the statelessness."
160	
161	**Bridge to Nick.** You have worked in regulated banking and know auth deeply. Frame at that level: "I've done bearer-token auth in regulated environments. In FastAPI the validation lives in a dependency that injects the authenticated principal, which is the same shape as a security filter populating the security context in Spring. The interesting part is always the revocation versus statelessness trade-off, which is why short expiries and refresh tokens exist."
162	
163	## Error handling with HTTPException
164	
165	**Mental model.** To return an error from a handler, you raise `HTTPException` with a status code and a detail message, and FastAPI turns it into a proper JSON error response. You can also register exception handlers that catch a given exception type globally and shape a consistent error response, so domain errors map cleanly to HTTP status codes.
166	
167	**Senior nuance.** The clean pattern is to raise domain exceptions deep in your code and have a single global exception handler translate them to HTTP responses at the edge, rather than scattering `HTTPException(status_code=...)` everywhere. That keeps your business logic free of HTTP concerns and gives you one consistent error contract. Validation errors are handled automatically (Pydantic produces structured 422s), so you only hand-handle your domain failures.
168	
169	**If they ask...**
170	
171	- *"How do you handle errors?"*
172	  "For a direct error I raise `HTTPException` with a status and detail and FastAPI serialises it. But the pattern I prefer is raising domain exceptions in the business logic and registering one global exception handler that maps them to HTTP responses at the edge. That keeps HTTP concerns out of the core logic and gives a single consistent error shape. Validation errors I get for free as structured 422s from Pydantic."
173	
174	**Bridge to Nick.** This is `@ControllerAdvice` / `@ExceptionHandler` in Spring, mapping domain exceptions to responses centrally. "I'd register a global handler that maps domain exceptions to HTTP responses, exactly like `@ControllerAdvice` in Spring, so the handlers stay clean."
175	
176	## Starlette and Uvicorn underpinnings, and the worker model
177	
178	**Mental model.** FastAPI is a thin, typed layer on top of Starlette, which is the actual ASGI framework doing routing, middleware, and request handling. Uvicorn is the ASGI server that runs the app, the thing that actually speaks HTTP and drives the event loop. In production you typically run multiple Uvicorn worker processes (often managed by Gunicorn or a process manager), each with its own event loop.
179	
180	**Senior nuance.** The scaling model is "processes for parallelism, async for concurrency." Each worker process has one event loop handling many concurrent requests via async; you add worker processes to use more CPU cores, because Python's GIL means one process effectively uses one core for CPU work. So you tune worker count to cores and rely on async within each worker for I/O concurrency. Understanding that two-level model (processes x async) is the depth signal.
181	
182	**If they ask...**
183	
184	- *"What's actually running your FastAPI app?"*
185	  "Uvicorn, the ASGI server, runs the app and drives the event loop. FastAPI itself is a typed layer over Starlette, which does the routing and middleware. In production I run several Uvicorn worker processes, each with its own event loop. The model is processes for parallelism across cores, async for concurrency within each process, because the GIL means one process is effectively one core for CPU work. So I size workers to cores and let async handle I/O concurrency inside each."
186	
187	**Bridge to Nick.** You have done containerised deploys on Cloud Run and you know horizontal scaling. "On Cloud Run I'd run Uvicorn workers per container and scale container instances horizontally. It's the same process-versus-async distinction as goroutines-within-a-process versus more pods in Go, just with the GIL constraint shaping how many workers per box."
188	
189	## Streaming responses / SSE: the critical one for AI apps
190	
191	**Mental model.** A streaming response sends the body incrementally instead of all at once. FastAPI supports this via a streaming response that consumes an async generator: you yield chunks and they go to the client as they are produced. Server-Sent Events (SSE) is a simple one-way streaming protocol over HTTP where the server pushes a sequence of events to the client on a long-lived connection.
192	
193	**Senior nuance: and why this matters for AI.** LLMs generate tokens one at a time. If you wait for the full completion before responding, the user stares at a spinner for many seconds. Streaming the tokens as they are generated is what makes AI chat feel responsive, the text appearing word by word. This is exactly where FastAPI's async model pays off: the async generator yields each token to the client while the event loop stays free, and SSE is the usual transport. For a flight-search-in-ChatGPT product, streaming is how partial results and model output reach the user without a long blocking wait. This is the single most important FastAPI concept to connect explicitly to AI work.
194	
195	**If they ask...**
196	
197	- *"Why does streaming matter for LLM applications?"*
198	  "Because LLMs produce tokens incrementally. If I buffer the whole completion before responding, the user waits seconds with nothing on screen. Streaming pushes each token as it's generated, so the response appears word by word and feels immediate. FastAPI does this with a streaming response over an async generator: I yield tokens as they arrive and the event loop stays free to serve other requests. Server-Sent Events is the usual transport. For something like flight search inside ChatGPT, streaming is what lets partial output and model tokens reach the user without a long blocking wait."
199	
200	- *"SSE versus WebSockets?"*
201	  "SSE is one-way, server to client, over plain HTTP, and it's simple, which is exactly right for streaming LLM output where the data flows one direction. WebSockets are full duplex and heavier, which you'd want for genuinely bidirectional realtime. For token streaming, SSE is usually the right, simpler choice."
202	
203	**Bridge to Nick.** You built generative-AI search APIs on Vertex AI and Gemini, and you know gRPC streaming. The connection is direct and strong: "I built generative search APIs on Vertex and Gemini, so token streaming is the production reality I worked in. gRPC has server-streaming for the same reason; SSE over HTTP is the web-native equivalent, and FastAPI's async generator is how you produce the stream. The whole async model exists to make this cheap." This is your strongest bridge in the whole doc; lean on it.
204	
205	## Testing with TestClient / httpx
206	
207	**Mental model.** FastAPI gives you a `TestClient` (built on httpx) that calls your app in-process, without starting a real server or opening a network socket. You write tests that make requests against your app and assert on responses. For async tests you use httpx's async client directly. Combined with dependency overrides, you can swap real dependencies for fakes in tests.
208	
209	**Senior nuance.** The high-value pattern is dependency-override testing: because routes declare their dependencies via `Depends`, your test overrides the database or auth dependency with a fake, then exercises the real route logic against it. That gives you fast, isolated tests of the actual handler without standing up real infrastructure. The depth signal is connecting DI to testability rather than treating testing as a separate concern.
210	
211	**If they ask...**
212	
213	- *"How do you test a FastAPI app?"*
214	  "With `TestClient`, which calls the app in-process over httpx, no real server needed. I make requests and assert on the responses. The powerful part is dependency overrides: because routes get their dependencies through `Depends`, I swap the real DB or auth dependency for a fake in the test and run the real handler logic against it. Fast, isolated, and it tests the actual route. For async-specific code I use the httpx async client directly."
215	
216	**Bridge to Nick.** You are a TDD practitioner, so this lands naturally. "I work test-first. The dependency-override pattern is what makes that clean in FastAPI: it's the same reason constructor injection makes Spring code testable, you inject fakes at the boundary. `TestClient` calling in-process is like MockMvc, no network, real handler."
217	
218	## FastAPI vs Flask vs Django REST: when to use which
219	
220	**Mental model.** Flask is minimal and synchronous (WSGI), a small core you extend; great for simple services but no built-in async, validation, or docs. Django REST Framework is heavyweight and batteries-included, built on Django's ORM and admin; great when you want a full opinionated stack with everything wired. FastAPI is the modern middle: async-native, typed, automatic validation and docs, lighter than Django but far more built-in than Flask. For typed, async, API-first AI services it is the obvious choice.
221	
222	**Senior nuance.** The decision is about what you are optimising for. Choose Django REST when you want a full opinionated framework with ORM, auth, and admin out of the box and you accept the weight. Choose Flask for a tiny, simple synchronous service where you want minimal dependencies. Choose FastAPI for high-concurrency, I/O-bound, typed API work, which is exactly AI services, because async plus Pydantic plus generated OpenAPI is precisely what those need. Articulating it as a fit-for-purpose trade-off rather than "FastAPI is best" is the mature answer.
223	
224	**If they ask...**
225	
226	- *"Why FastAPI over Flask or Django REST?"*
227	  "It depends on the job. Django REST when I want a full batteries-included stack, ORM, admin, auth, and I accept the weight. Flask for a tiny synchronous service with minimal dependencies. FastAPI for typed, async, high-concurrency API work, which is exactly AI services, because async handles the I/O-bound LLM and network waits, Pydantic gives me validated typed contracts, and OpenAPI docs come for free. For an AI service team it's the natural fit; for a CMS-style app Django might win."
228	
229	**Bridge to Nick.** You evaluate tools on fit, leverage, and trade-offs, which is exactly the framing interviewers reward. "I pick frameworks on fit. For an I/O-bound, typed, API-first AI service, FastAPI's async model and generated contracts are the leverage. I'd reach for Django REST if the job were a full content-managed product, and Flask if it were genuinely trivial."
230	
231	---
232	
233	# PART 2: MCP and FastMCP
234	
235	## What the Model Context Protocol (MCP) is
236	
237	**Mental model.** MCP is an open standard, originally from Anthropic, for connecting LLMs to external tools, data, and prompts through a client-server model. The LLM application (the host, like ChatGPT or Claude) runs an MCP client; your capabilities live in an MCP server. The protocol standardises how the model discovers what a server offers and how it calls into it. The slogan is that it is "USB-C for AI": one standard interface so any compliant model can use any compliant server.
238	
239	**Senior nuance.** The reason MCP matters is the N-times-M problem. Without a standard, every model integration with every tool is a bespoke connector, so M models times N tools is M-times-N custom integrations. MCP collapses that: build one MCP server and any MCP-capable model can use it, build one client and it can use any server. It is the same standardisation argument as adopting a protocol like HTTP or gRPC instead of bespoke RPC per pair. That framing is the depth signal.
240	
241	**If they ask...**
242	
243	- *"What is MCP, in your own words?"*
244	  "It's an open standard from Anthropic for connecting LLMs to external tools and data through a client-server model. The model's host app runs an MCP client, and my capabilities live in an MCP server. The protocol defines how the model discovers what the server offers and calls into it. The value is standardisation: instead of a bespoke connector for every model-tool pair, I build one server and any MCP-capable model can use it. It's the N-by-M integration problem solved by a common protocol, the same way HTTP standardised web communication."
245	
246	**Bridge to Nick.** You know protocols deeply, gRPC, Protobuf, REST. The framing writes itself: "I think of MCP as a protocol standardisation play, the same logic as choosing gRPC with a shared schema over bespoke RPC. Define the contract once and any client speaks it. MCP does that for the model-to-tool boundary."
247	
248	## The three MCP primitives: tools, resources, prompts
249	
250	**Mental model.** An MCP server can expose three kinds of thing. Tools are functions the model can call to take an action or fetch dynamic data (search flights, get reward seats). Resources are read-only data the model can load for context, addressed by a URI, like files or records. Prompts are reusable, parameterised prompt templates the server offers to the client. The distinction is roughly: tools do, resources inform, prompts guide.
251	
252	**Senior nuance.** The control distinction matters. Tools are model-controlled: the model decides when to call them based on the conversation. Resources are more application or user-controlled: they are context to be loaded, not actions the model autonomously invokes. Knowing that tools are the active, model-invoked primitive, and that flight search would be a tool rather than a resource, is the signal you understand the model, not just the vocabulary.
253	
254	**If they ask...**
255	
256	- *"What are the MCP primitives?"*
257	  "Three. Tools are functions the model can call to do something or fetch dynamic data, like searching flights. Resources are read-only data the model loads for context, addressed by URI. Prompts are reusable parameterised prompt templates the server offers. Tools do, resources inform, prompts guide. The key distinction is control: tools are model-invoked, the model decides when to call them, while resources are context to load. For an airline, flight search is a tool, because it's an action the model takes."
258	
259	**Bridge to Nick.** Map to your API instincts: "Tools are like POST-style action endpoints the model can invoke, resources are like GET-able read-only data it can pull in, and prompts are server-supplied templates. As an API designer I'd model flight search as a tool, an action with typed inputs and outputs, not a static resource."
260	
261	## What FastMCP is
262	
263	**Mental model.** FastMCP is a Pythonic, decorator-based framework for building MCP servers, deliberately designed to feel like FastAPI. You write a normal Python function, decorate it to expose it as an MCP tool (or resource, or prompt), and FastMCP handles the protocol: the discovery, the schema, the request/response wiring. Your type hints and docstring become the tool's schema and description that the model sees.
264	
265	**Senior nuance.** The deliberate FastAPI-likeness is the whole point and a great thing to name: same decorator ergonomics, same use of Python type hints to define the contract, same automatic schema generation. So everything you know about Pydantic-typed FastAPI handlers transfers directly. The depth signal is recognising that the function signature and docstring are not just code, they are the interface the model reasons over, so writing them clearly is part of making the tool usable by the LLM.
266	
267	**If they ask...**
268	
269	- *"What is FastMCP?"*
270	  "It's a Pythonic framework for building MCP servers, deliberately shaped like FastAPI. I write a normal function, decorate it to expose it as an MCP tool, and FastMCP handles all the protocol plumbing, discovery, schema, request and response. The type hints and docstring become the tool's schema and description that the model sees. So if you know FastAPI, FastMCP is immediately familiar: same decorator style, same type-hints-as-contract idea."
271	
272	- *"What's the relationship between the type hints and the model?"*
273	  "They're the interface. The model only knows about my tool through its name, description, and parameter schema, and FastMCP generates that schema from my type hints and docstring. So writing a clear signature and docstring isn't cosmetic, it's how I make the tool legible to the model so it calls it correctly with the right arguments."
274	
275	**Bridge to Nick.** This is your strongest conceptual reuse. "FastMCP is FastAPI's ergonomics applied to MCP. The decorator-plus-type-hints pattern is identical, and the type hints generate the tool schema the same way they generate OpenAPI in FastAPI. So my FastAPI mental model carries straight over; the difference is the consumer is an LLM, not an HTTP client."
276	
277	## Transports: stdio for local, streamable HTTP / SSE for remote
278	
279	**Mental model.** MCP servers talk to clients over a transport. For a local server running on the same machine as the client (a desktop app launching a subprocess), the transport is stdio: the client and server exchange messages over standard input and output. For a remote server reached over the network, the transport is HTTP-based, using streamable HTTP / SSE so the server can stream responses back. Local equals stdio, remote equals HTTP.
280	
281	**Senior nuance.** The transport choice follows the deployment topology. stdio is for the desktop case where the host process spawns the server as a child process and pipes to it, no network, no auth needed. Streamable HTTP / SSE is for a hosted server multiple clients reach over the network, which is what a ChatGPT App is. The streaming part matters because, just like FastAPI, the server streams results back over a long-lived HTTP connection. Knowing which transport goes with which topology, and that the remote case is the one that needs network auth, is the depth signal.
282	
283	**If they ask...**
284	
285	- *"How does an MCP client talk to a server?"*
286	  "Over a transport, and the transport follows the topology. If the server runs locally as a subprocess of the host app, it's stdio, messages over standard in and out, no network. If the server is remote, reached over the network, it's HTTP-based, streamable HTTP or SSE, so the server can stream responses back. Local is stdio, remote is HTTP. A ChatGPT App is the remote HTTP case, which is also where you need auth because it's exposed over the network."
287	
288	**Bridge to Nick.** You know HTTP, SSE, and process IO well. "stdio transport is just piping over a child process's stdin/stdout, the local IPC case. The remote case is HTTP with SSE for streaming, which is the same streaming-over-HTTP pattern as FastAPI. So a remote MCP server is, under the hood, a streaming HTTP service."
289	
290	## How a remote MCP server becomes a "ChatGPT App" / connector
291	
292	**Mental model.** OpenAI's ChatGPT Apps platform is MCP-based. You build a remote MCP server that exposes your tools over streamable HTTP, register it with ChatGPT as a connector/app, and ChatGPT becomes the MCP client. When a user's conversation calls for your capability, ChatGPT discovers and calls your tools. So "a ChatGPT App" is, technically, a remote MCP server that ChatGPT connects to. That is almost certainly exactly what Virgin's flight-search-in-ChatGPT is.
293	
294	**Senior nuance.** The architectural point: your server doesn't know about ChatGPT specifically, it just speaks MCP, and ChatGPT is one MCP client among potentially many. The same server could be exposed to Claude or any MCP host. That decoupling is the value of building on the standard rather than a proprietary plugin format. For Virgin, it means one MCP server for flight search could serve ChatGPT today and other AI surfaces later without rebuilding.
295	
296	**If they ask...**
297	
298	- *"What is a ChatGPT App, technically?"*
299	  "It's a remote MCP server that ChatGPT connects to as the client. OpenAI's Apps platform is MCP-based, so you build an MCP server exposing your tools over streamable HTTP, register it as a connector, and ChatGPT discovers and calls those tools during a conversation. My server just speaks MCP, it doesn't know about ChatGPT specifically, which means the same server could serve other MCP hosts too. For Virgin's flight search in ChatGPT, that's almost certainly what's running underneath: a FastMCP server exposing flight-search tools that ChatGPT calls."
300	
301	**Bridge to Nick.** Strategic framing, which is your strength: "Building on MCP rather than a proprietary plugin is an optionality play. One server, standard protocol, multiple AI front-ends over time. That's exactly the kind of leverage-and-optionality argument I'd make in a design review, and it's why an airline would build flight search as an MCP server rather than a one-off ChatGPT integration."
302	
303	## Auth for remote MCP (OAuth)
304	
305	**Mental model.** A remote MCP server is exposed over the network, so it needs authentication, and the MCP standard uses OAuth for this. The client obtains an OAuth token and presents it to the MCP server, which validates it before allowing tool calls. This is how a hosted server knows which user is making a request and whether they are allowed to.
306	
307	**Senior nuance.** This connects straight back to the FastAPI auth section: it is the same bearer-token, dependency-validated pattern, just at the MCP boundary. For something like reward seats, you need the authenticated user's identity to return their specific entitlements, so OAuth is not optional, it is how the tool call is scoped to the right account. Recognising that remote MCP auth is the same OAuth/JWT machinery you already discussed, applied to the tool boundary, ties the two halves of the interview together.
308	
309	**If they ask...**
310	
311	- *"How is a remote MCP server secured?"*
312	  "With OAuth, which the MCP standard supports. The client gets a token and presents it to the server, and the server validates it before allowing tool calls. It's the same bearer-token pattern as a normal API, applied at the MCP boundary. It matters for anything user-specific, reward seats for example, because the server needs the authenticated identity to return that user's entitlements. So OAuth scopes the tool call to the right account."
313	
314	**Bridge to Nick.** "It's the same auth machinery I described for FastAPI, OAuth and bearer tokens validated server-side, just at the tool boundary instead of a REST endpoint. Given my regulated-banking background, the interesting part is the same: scoping each call to the authenticated principal and keeping tokens short-lived."
315	
316	## Why an airline would build flight search as an MCP server
317	
318	**Mental model.** An airline exposes its core capabilities, search flights, get reward seats, as MCP tools so that an LLM can call them on a customer's behalf inside a conversational surface like ChatGPT. The model handles the natural-language understanding ("find me a flight to Sydney next Friday under 200 dollars"), then calls the typed `search_flights` tool with structured parameters, gets structured results back, and presents them. The airline owns the tool and the data; the model orchestrates.
319	
320	**Senior nuance.** The clean separation is the point: the LLM does language and orchestration, the MCP tool does the deterministic, authoritative business logic and data access. You do not want the model inventing flight prices; you want it calling a real, typed, validated tool that returns real inventory. So MCP tools are the trustworthy, deterministic layer under the probabilistic model. That "deterministic tool under a probabilistic model" framing is exactly the kind of architectural maturity that signals depth.
321	
322	**If they ask...**
323	
324	- *"Why would an airline build flight search as an MCP server?"*
325	  "So an LLM can call their real flight-search capability on a customer's behalf inside something like ChatGPT. The model does the language part, understands 'find me a flight to Sydney under 200 dollars', then calls a typed `search_flights` tool with structured parameters and gets real inventory back. The airline owns the tool and the data; the model just orchestrates. The important design point is the separation: the model is probabilistic and handles language, the tool is deterministic and handles the authoritative business logic and pricing. You never want the model inventing prices, you want it calling a real validated tool. MCP is how you expose that tool to any AI surface."
326	
327	**Bridge to Nick.** Pull together API design, typed contracts, and your event-driven/regulated instincts: "I'd design `search_flights` and `get_reward_seats` as typed tools with validated inputs and structured outputs, the same discipline as any API I'd build. The architecture I'd argue for is the deterministic, authoritative tool layer sitting under the probabilistic model, so the model orchestrates language but the real inventory and pricing come from a trustworthy service. That's a clean separation of concerns, and it's exactly why MCP fits an airline."
328	
329	## A tiny FastMCP tool sketch (to recognise, not memorise)
330	
331	You will not be coding, but being able to picture this makes you fluent. The shape:
332	
333	```python
334	from fastmcp import FastMCP
335	
336	mcp = FastMCP("flight-search")
337	
338	@mcp.tool()
339	def search_flights(origin: str, destination: str, date: str, max_price: float | None = None) -> list[dict]:
340	    """Search available flights between two airports on a given date.
341	
342	    origin: IATA code, e.g. MEL
343	    destination: IATA code, e.g. SYD
344	    date: ISO date, e.g. 2026-07-01
345	    max_price: optional cap on fare in AUD
346	    """
347	    results = flight_backend.query(origin, destination, date, max_price)
348	    return results
349	```
350	
351	What to notice, and what to say if asked to talk through it:
352	
353	- The `@mcp.tool()` decorator exposes the function as an MCP tool. "It's the FastAPI decorator pattern, the decorator registers the function and FastMCP handles the protocol."
354	- The type hints (`origin: str`, `max_price: float | None`) become the tool's input schema the model sees. "The type hints are the contract, same as Pydantic in FastAPI; the model gets a typed schema from them."
355	- The docstring becomes the tool's description the model reads to decide when and how to call it. "The docstring isn't just documentation, it's what the model reads to understand the tool, so I write it for the model."
356	- The return type structures the output. "Typed in, typed out, the model orchestrates, the tool does the real query."
357	
358	If asked "could you build one of these?", the honest, confident answer: "Yes. It's a decorated, type-hinted Python function, which is the FastAPI pattern I know well. The framework-specific learning is small because FastMCP deliberately mirrors FastAPI; the real work is designing good typed tool contracts and clear descriptions so the model uses them correctly, which is API design, which is my strength."
359	
360	---
361	
362	# Closing framing for the conversation
363	
364	Two things to hold in your head so you sound grounded rather than rehearsed:
365	
366	1. You are not claiming FastAPI/FastMCP production experience, and you do not need to. The honest, strong position is: "I haven't shipped FastAPI in production, but the concepts map cleanly onto what I've built in Spring and Go, async, DI, typed contracts, streaming, auth, so I'm confident I'd be productive fast. FastMCP is FastAPI's pattern applied to MCP, and I understand the protocol and why an airline exposes flight search as MCP tools to ChatGPT." That is a senior answer: it shows transferable depth and intellectual honesty, which is exactly the Strong Opinions Loosely Held register you operate in.
367	
368	2. Every FastAPI concept has a Spring or Go twin, and every MCP concept is a protocol-and-API-design problem you already think in. When in doubt, reach for the bridge: name the thing you already know, then map it. That keeps you answering from genuine ground instead of reciting.

# FastAPI and FastMCP Fundamentals: Interview Brushup

This is a confidence-and-articulation doc, not a reference manual: read each topic's mental model and the "speakable" answers out loud until you can say them in your own words without notes. You know REST, gRPC, HTTP, DI, and async deeply already, so most of this is mapping concepts you own onto Python names, not learning new ideas.

## How FastAPI and FastMCP connect to the Virgin role

Virgin's CIO/AI team runs a live flight-search experience inside ChatGPT, built on OpenAI's ChatGPT Apps platform. ChatGPT Apps are MCP-based: the app is a remote MCP server that exposes tools (like flight search) which the model calls on the user's behalf. FastMCP is the Pythonic framework for building those MCP servers, and it is deliberately shaped like FastAPI. So the stack is almost certainly: FastAPI for normal HTTP/AI service endpoints, FastMCP for the tools ChatGPT calls, both async, both Pydantic-typed. If you can talk about FastAPI's async model and Pydantic, FastMCP follows naturally, because it reuses the same mental furniture.

The one-sentence version to have ready: "FastAPI is the async Python web framework for building the AI service APIs, and FastMCP is the same idea applied to MCP, so the flight-search tools Virgin exposes to ChatGPT are almost certainly FastMCP tools."

---

# PART 1: FastAPI

## ASGI vs WSGI, and why async matters

**Mental model.** WSGI is the old synchronous Python web standard: one worker handles one request at a time, blocking until it finishes. ASGI is the async successor: a single worker can hold thousands of in-flight requests, suspending each one while it waits on I/O and doing other work in the meantime. FastAPI is built on ASGI, which is what lets it handle high-concurrency I/O-bound workloads (calling an LLM, hitting a database, fanning out to other services) on a small number of workers.

**Senior nuance.** Async only helps when you are I/O-bound, not CPU-bound. The whole point is the event loop reclaims the thread while you wait on the network. If you do heavy CPU work inside an async handler, you block the event loop and stall every other concurrent request on that worker. For AI workloads this matters enormously: an LLM call can take many seconds, and during that wait one async worker can serve hundreds of other requests instead of sitting idle.

**If they ask...**

- *"Why is FastAPI async, and when does that actually help?"*
  "Because it is built on ASGI rather than the old synchronous WSGI standard. The benefit is concurrency on I/O-bound work. When a handler is waiting on a slow network call, the event loop frees the thread to serve other requests instead of blocking. For AI services that is the dominant case: you spend most of your time waiting on an LLM or a database, so a few async workers can hold a lot of concurrent requests. It does not speed up CPU-bound work, it just stops you wasting threads on waiting."

- *"What happens if you do something slow and synchronous inside an async route?"*
  "You block the event loop. The whole worker stops servicing other requests until that blocking call returns, so your concurrency collapses. The fix is either make it genuinely async, or push it off the event loop, for example onto a thread pool or a background worker."

**Bridge to Nick.** This is the same reasoning you already apply in Go. Go's goroutines and async I/O exist for exactly this: don't block a thread waiting on the network. ASGI is Python catching up to what Go gave you natively. When you talk about it, you can frame it as "this is the goroutine intuition, just expressed through an event loop instead of the runtime scheduler."

## async/await handlers and the sync-route threadpool trap

**Mental model.** In FastAPI you write a route as either `async def` or plain `def`. An `async def` route runs directly on the event loop, so you must only `await` non-blocking things inside it. A plain `def` route is the escape hatch: FastAPI runs it in a thread pool so a blocking call inside it does not freeze the loop.

**Senior nuance.** The trap is mixing them up. If you write `async def` but then call a blocking, synchronous library inside it (a sync database driver, `requests`, `time.sleep`), you block the event loop and silently kill concurrency. The counterintuitive rule: if your dependency is blocking and you have no async version, a plain `def` route is safer than an `async def` one, because FastAPI offloads the `def` route to a thread. People assume `async` is always faster and reach for it reflexively, which is the actual footgun.

**If they ask...**

- *"When would you use a normal `def` route instead of `async def`?"*
  "When the work inside is blocking and I have no async-native library for it. FastAPI runs plain `def` routes in a thread pool, so a blocking call there doesn't stall the event loop. If I forced it into an `async def` and called the blocking thing directly, I would freeze the loop. So `async def` for genuinely async work, plain `def` for blocking work I can't make async."

- *"Common async mistake you have seen?"*
  "Writing `async def` and then calling a synchronous client inside it, like a blocking HTTP library. It looks async, it passes tests, and under load the throughput is terrible because every one of those calls blocks the loop. The tell is that concurrency doesn't scale even though everything says async."

**Bridge to Nick.** In Spring you mostly think per-request-thread (servlet model), so blocking is fine because each request has its own thread. FastAPI's `def` route in a thread pool is essentially that Spring model on demand, while `async def` is the new event-loop model. You can say: "the plain `def` route gives me the per-thread Spring behaviour when I need it, and `async def` is for the event-loop path."

## Pydantic models for request/response validation and serialisation

**Mental model.** Pydantic is the typed data layer. You declare a class with typed fields, and FastAPI uses it to validate and parse the incoming JSON body automatically, rejecting bad input with a structured 422 error before your code runs. The same models serialise your responses back to JSON. It is schema-as-code: the type annotations are the contract.

**Senior nuance.** Pydantic isn't just validation, it is the single source of truth that also generates the OpenAPI schema and the docs. One model definition gives you parsing, validation, serialisation, editor autocompletion, and API documentation. The depth signal is knowing the boundary discipline: you validate and coerce at the edge of the system, so everything inside your handler is already a typed, trusted object, never a raw dict.

**If they ask...**

- *"What does Pydantic give you?"*
  "Typed request and response models. I declare a class with typed fields, and FastAPI validates the incoming JSON against it automatically. Bad input gets rejected with a structured error before my handler runs, and the same model serialises the response. The nice part is one definition drives validation, serialisation, and the OpenAPI schema, so the types are the contract."

- *"How is that different from just parsing a dict?"*
  "With a dict, every field access is an assumption that could be wrong at runtime, and validation is scattered. With Pydantic the validation happens once at the boundary, and inside the handler I'm working with a typed object I can trust. It moves the failure to the edge where it belongs and gives me an explicit, documented contract."

**Bridge to Nick.** This is DTO validation, the same pattern as Bean Validation / `@Valid` on a request DTO in Spring, or a typed struct with validation in Go. Frame it directly: "Pydantic is DTO validation. It's the `@Valid` annotated request DTO from Spring, except the type annotations also generate the OpenAPI schema for free." That instantly shows you understand it as a known pattern, not a novelty.

## Dependency injection via Depends

**Mental model.** FastAPI's `Depends` is its dependency injection mechanism. You declare a dependency (a function that produces something, like a database session, the current user, or a config object) and FastAPI resolves it and injects the result into your handler. Dependencies can depend on other dependencies, and FastAPI caches and wires the whole graph per request.

**Senior nuance.** Depends is how you do cross-cutting concerns cleanly: auth, database sessions, pagination params, rate-limit checks. The elegant bit is that a dependency can `yield`, which lets it run setup before the request and teardown after (open a DB session, yield it, close it on the way out), so it doubles as scoped resource management. The depth point: this is constructor injection done per-request, and it keeps handlers thin and testable because you can override any dependency in tests.

**If they ask...**

- *"How does dependency injection work in FastAPI?"*
  "Through `Depends`. I write a function that produces a dependency, like a database session or the authenticated user, and declare it as a parameter on the route. FastAPI resolves the dependency graph per request and injects the results. Dependencies can depend on each other, and one that uses `yield` can do setup and teardown around the request, so it handles scoped resources like a DB session cleanly."

- *"Why is that useful for testing?"*
  "Because I can override any dependency. In a test I swap the real database dependency for a fake or an in-memory one without touching the handler. The handler just declares what it needs, so I control what gets injected. It keeps the handler thin and the wiring explicit."

**Bridge to Nick.** This is the DI container you already know from Spring, just request-scoped and function-based instead of annotation-and-bean-based. Say it plainly: "`Depends` is the DI container. It is Spring's `@Autowired` and bean wiring, but resolved per request as a function graph, and the `yield` form is basically a scoped bean with a destroy method." Spring engineers immediately get this.

## Path, query, and body params

**Mental model.** FastAPI infers where each parameter comes from by its type and declaration. A parameter named in the route path (like `/flights/{id}`) is a path param. A simple scalar not in the path becomes a query param. A Pydantic model parameter is read from the request body. You rarely have to say which is which; the function signature declares the whole input contract.

**Senior nuance.** Because the parameter types drive parsing, validation, and the OpenAPI schema all at once, your function signature is the API spec. You can add constraints inline (a query param with a max length, an integer with a minimum) and those become both runtime validation and documented schema. The signal is understanding that there is no separate "parse the request" step; the typed signature is the parsing layer.

**If they ask...**

## response_model and automatic OpenAPI/Swagger docs

**Mental model.** `response_model` declares the Pydantic type of what a route returns. FastAPI uses it to serialise the response, and crucially to filter it: anything not in the response model is stripped out, so you can return a rich internal object and only expose the declared fields. Separately, FastAPI generates an OpenAPI schema from all your types and serves interactive Swagger UI and ReDoc docs automatically, with zero extra code.

**Senior nuance.** `response_model` is a security and contract tool, not just serialisation. Declaring an output model means you cannot accidentally leak internal fields (a password hash, an internal flag) even if your handler returns an object that has them, because the response model defines the allow-list. The depth signal: input and output models are deliberately different types, so the shape you accept is decoupled from the shape you return.

**If they ask...**

FastAPI filters the response down to exactly the fields in the model, so even if my handler returns an object carrying extra internal fields, only the declared ones go out. That stops accidental data leaks, and it documents the response shape in OpenAPI. I usually keep the input and output models separate so the accepted shape and the returned shape are independent."

## Middleware

**Mental model.** Middleware wraps every request and response, running code before the handler and after it. You use it for cross-cutting concerns that apply globally: logging, request timing, adding headers, CORS, correlation IDs, catching and shaping errors. It sits in the request pipeline around your routes.

**Senior nuance.** The distinction worth knowing: middleware is for truly global, per-request concerns; `Depends` is for per-route, injectable concerns. Use middleware for things like attaching a trace ID to every request and logging latency; use Depends for auth and resource scoping that vary by route. Reaching for middleware when you meant a dependency (or vice versa) is the common design smell.

**If they ask...**

- *"Middleware versus a dependency, when do you use which?"*
  "Middleware for global, per-request concerns that wrap everything: request logging, timing, CORS, attaching a correlation ID. Dependencies for per-route concerns I want injected and testable: auth, a DB session, pagination. If it applies to every request uniformly and doesn't need to be injected into the handler, it's middleware; if a specific route needs it as a value, it's a dependency."

**Bridge to Nick.** This is servlet filters / Spring interceptors, or Go HTTP middleware chains. You have built observability with OpenTelemetry, so frame it: "Middleware is where I'd wire request-level OpenTelemetry spans and correlation IDs, same place I'd put a filter in Spring or a middleware in a Go handler chain."

## Background tasks

**Mental model.** A background task lets a handler schedule work to run after the response is sent. The client gets its response immediately, and FastAPI runs the task afterwards in the same process. Typical uses: send a confirmation email, write an audit log, invalidate a cache, things the caller doesn't need to wait for.

**Senior nuance.** Background tasks run in-process and are fire-and-forget with no durability. If the process dies, the task is lost; there is no retry, no persistence. So they are right for low-stakes, best-effort follow-ups, and wrong for anything that must not be lost, which belongs on a real queue or worker (Celery, a Pub/Sub consumer, etc.). Knowing that boundary is the senior signal.

**If they ask...**

## Startup/shutdown lifespan

**Mental model.** The lifespan handler runs code once when the app starts and once when it shuts down. You use it to set up and tear down shared resources: open a database connection pool, initialise an HTTP client or an LLM client, load a model into memory on startup, and close all of it cleanly on shutdown.

**Senior nuance.** The modern API is a single `lifespan` async context manager (setup before `yield`, teardown after), which replaced the older separate startup/shutdown event handlers. The reason it matters for AI services: you want to create the LLM client, connection pool, or load a model once at boot and reuse it across requests, not per-request. Per-request setup of an expensive client is a classic performance bug.

## Auth: OAuth2 password flow and JWT bearer

**Mental model.** FastAPI ships OAuth2 helpers. The password flow takes a username and password at a token endpoint and issues a token, typically a JWT. On every subsequent request the client sends that JWT as a bearer token in the Authorization header. A dependency validates the token (checks signature and expiry, decodes the claims) and injects the current user, so any route can require auth just by depending on it.

**Senior nuance.** JWTs are stateless and self-contained, which is the strength and the trap. The server can verify a JWT without a database lookup because the signature proves it is valid, but that also means you cannot easily revoke one before it expires. So you keep token lifetimes short and use refresh tokens for longer sessions. Knowing the revocation trade-off is the depth signal; lots of people can wire JWT auth but fewer can articulate why short expiries and refresh tokens exist.

Then any protected route just depends on that, so auth is declarative per route."

- *"What's the downside of JWTs?"*
  "They're stateless, so I can verify them without a database hit, but I also can't easily revoke one before it expires, because validity is just the signature. So I keep access tokens short-lived and use refresh tokens for longer sessions. If I genuinely need instant revocation I'd need a denylist or a stateful session, which gives back some of the statelessness."

**Bridge to Nick.** You have worked in regulated banking and know auth deeply. Frame at that level: "I've done bearer-token auth in regulated environments. ## Error handling with HTTPException

**Mental model.** To return an error from a handler, you raise `HTTPException` with a status code and a detail message, and FastAPI turns it into a proper JSON error response. You can also register exception handlers that catch a given exception type globally and shape a consistent error response, so domain errors map cleanly to HTTP status codes.

**Senior nuance.** The clean pattern is to raise domain exceptions deep in your code and have a single global exception handler translate them to HTTP responses at the edge, rather than scattering `HTTPException(status_code=...)` everywhere. That keeps your business logic free of HTTP concerns and gives you one consistent error contract. Validation errors are handled automatically (Pydantic produces structured 422s), so you only hand-handle your domain failures.

## Starlette and Uvicorn underpinnings, and the worker model

**Mental model.** FastAPI is a thin, typed layer on top of Starlette, which is the actual ASGI framework doing routing, middleware, and request handling. Uvicorn is the ASGI server that runs the app, the thing that actually speaks HTTP and drives the event loop. In production you typically run multiple Uvicorn worker processes (often managed by Gunicorn or a process manager), each with its own event loop.

**Senior nuance.** The scaling model is "processes for parallelism, async for concurrency." Each worker process has one event loop handling many concurrent requests via async; you add worker processes to use more CPU cores, because Python's GIL means one process effectively uses one core for CPU work. So you tune worker count to cores and rely on async within each worker for I/O concurrency. Understanding that two-level model (processes x async) is the depth signal.

## Streaming responses / SSE: the critical one for AI apps

**Mental model.** A streaming response sends the body incrementally instead of all at once. FastAPI supports this via a streaming response that consumes an async generator: you yield chunks and they go to the client as they are produced. Server-Sent Events (SSE) is a simple one-way streaming protocol over HTTP where the server pushes a sequence of events to the client on a long-lived connection.

**Senior nuance: and why this matters for AI.** LLMs generate tokens one at a time. If you wait for the full completion before responding, the user stares at a spinner for many seconds. Streaming the tokens as they are generated is what makes AI chat feel responsive, the text appearing word by word. This is exactly where FastAPI's async model pays off: the async generator yields each token to the client while the event loop stays free, and SSE is the usual transport. For a flight-search-in-ChatGPT product, streaming is how partial results and model output reach the user without a long blocking wait. This is the single most important FastAPI concept to connect explicitly to AI work.

For something like flight search inside ChatGPT, streaming is what lets partial output and model tokens reach the user without a long blocking wait."

**Mental model.** Flask is minimal and synchronous (WSGI), a small core you extend; great for simple services but no built-in async, validation, or docs. # PART 2: MCP and FastMCP

## What the Model Context Protocol (MCP) is

**Mental model.** MCP is an open standard, originally from Anthropic, for connecting LLMs to external tools, data, and prompts through a client-server model. The LLM application (the host, like ChatGPT or Claude) runs an MCP client; your capabilities live in an MCP server. The protocol standardises how the model discovers what a server offers and how it calls into it. The slogan is that it is "USB-C for AI": one standard interface so any compliant model can use any compliant server.

**Senior nuance.** The reason MCP matters is the N-times-M problem. Without a standard, every model integration with every tool is a bespoke connector, so M models times N tools is M-times-N custom integrations. MCP collapses that: build one MCP server and any MCP-capable model can use it, build one client and it can use any server. It is the same standardisation argument as adopting a protocol like HTTP or gRPC instead of bespoke RPC per pair. That framing is the depth signal.

**If they ask...**

- *"What is MCP, in your own words?"*
  "It's an open standard from Anthropic for connecting LLMs to external tools and data through a client-server model. The model's host app runs an MCP client, and my capabilities live in an MCP server. The protocol defines how the model discovers what the server offers and calls into it. The value is standardisation: instead of a bespoke connector for every model-tool pair, I build one server and any MCP-capable model can use it. It's the N-by-M integration problem solved by a common protocol, the same way HTTP standardised web communication."

**Bridge to Nick.** You know protocols deeply, gRPC, Protobuf, REST. The framing writes itself: "I think of MCP as a protocol standardisation play, the same logic as choosing gRPC with a shared schema over bespoke RPC. Define the contract once and any client speaks it. MCP does that for the model-to-tool boundary."

## The three MCP primitives: tools, resources, prompts

**Mental model.** An MCP server can expose three kinds of thing. Tools are functions the model can call to take an action or fetch dynamic data (search flights, get reward seats). Resources are read-only data the model can load for context, addressed by a URI, like files or records. Prompts are reusable, parameterised prompt templates the server offers to the client. The distinction is roughly: tools do, resources inform, prompts guide.

**Senior nuance.** The control distinction matters. Tools are model-controlled: the model decides when to call them based on the conversation. Resources are more application or user-controlled: they are context to be loaded, not actions the model autonomously invokes. Knowing that tools are the active, model-invoked primitive, and that flight search would be a tool rather than a resource, is the signal you understand the model, not just the vocabulary.

**If they ask...**

- *"What are the MCP primitives?"*

Prompts are reusable parameterised prompt templates the server offers. Tools do, resources inform, prompts guide. The key distinction is control: tools are model-invoked, the model decides when to call them, while resources are context to load. For an airline, flight search is a tool, because it's an action the model takes."

**Bridge to Nick.** Map to your API instincts: "Tools are like POST-style action endpoints the model can invoke, resources are like GET-able read-only data it can pull in, and prompts are server-supplied templates. As an API designer I'd model flight search as a tool, an action with typed inputs and outputs, not a static resource."

## What FastMCP is

**Mental model.** FastMCP is a Pythonic, decorator-based framework for building MCP servers, deliberately designed to feel like FastAPI. You write a normal Python function, decorate it to expose it as an MCP tool (or resource, or prompt), and FastMCP handles the protocol: the discovery, the schema, the request/response wiring. Your type hints and docstring become the tool's schema and description that the model sees.

**Senior nuance.** The deliberate FastAPI-likeness is the whole point and a great thing to name: same decorator ergonomics, same use of Python type hints to define the contract, same automatic schema generation. So everything you know about Pydantic-typed FastAPI handlers transfers directly. The depth signal is recognising that the function signature and docstring are not just code, they are the interface the model reasons over, so writing them clearly is part of making the tool usable by the LLM.

## Transports: stdio for local, streamable HTTP / SSE for remote

**Mental model.** MCP servers talk to clients over a transport. For a local server running on the same machine as the client (a desktop app launching a subprocess), the transport is stdio: the client and server exchange messages over standard input and output. For a remote server reached over the network, the transport is HTTP-based, using streamable HTTP / SSE so the server can stream responses back. Local equals stdio, remote equals HTTP.

**Senior nuance.** The transport choice follows the deployment topology. stdio is for the desktop case where the host process spawns the server as a child process and pipes to it, no network, no auth needed. Streamable HTTP / SSE is for a hosted server multiple clients reach over the network, which is what a ChatGPT App is. The streaming part matters because, just like FastAPI, the server streams results back over a long-lived HTTP connection. Knowing which transport goes with which topology, and that the remote case is the one that needs network auth, is the depth signal.
